• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Bringing down, raising up﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 3], because He raises up peoples whose status was lowly in this world, and brings down peoples who were kings in this world and had lofty standing,

• and His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghāfir: 16].

A parallel to this verse mentioned is His saying: ﴿And they are pelted from every side, repelled, and for them is a perpetual (wāṣib) punishment﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 8–9], i.e., lasting. It was also said: a painful, agonizing punishment. The Arabs use waṣab for illness, and wuṣūb for permanence. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that when Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked him about His saying ﴿And to Him belongs religion, perpetually﴾ [al-Naḥl: 52], he said to him: "Wāṣib means lasting," and he cited the verse of Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt al-Thaqafī: (p-384)

*And to Him belongs religion, perpetually, and to Him belongs the dominion, and praise to Him in every state.*

From this is the saying of al-Duʾalī:

*I do not seek the little praise whose endurance, for a day, is with blame of time, all of it, lasting.*

Among those who said that the meaning of wāṣib in this verse is lasting: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Maymūn ibn Mihrān, al-Suddī, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās that "wāṣiban" means obligatory. And from Mujāhid also: "wāṣiban" means sincere. According to this saying of Mujāhid, the statement is in the sense of an imperative: i.e., fear lest you associate anything with Me, and devote obedience to Me sincerely. On this view the verse is like:

• His saying: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 83],

• His saying: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾ [al-Zumar: 3],

• His saying: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5],

• and His saying: "wāṣiban" [al-Naḥl: 52], a state (ḥāl) in which the adverb operates.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then is it other than Allah you fear?﴾. In this noble verse, He, exalted is He, denounces those who fear other than Him, because only the one in whose hand is all benefit and all harm should be feared. Indeed, others cannot benefit you with anything God has not willed for you, nor can they harm you with anything God has not decreed upon you.

He, exalted is He, has here indicated that the denunciation of fearing other than Allah is because it is Allah who is hoped for benefit and feared for harm. For this reason He followed His saying ﴿Then is it other than Allah you fear?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 52] with His saying: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah; then when harm touches you, to Him you cry out﴾ [al-Naḥl: 53]. The meaning of "tajʾarūn" (you cry out) is that you raise your voices in supplication and appeal for help when calamities descend. From this is the saying of al-Aʿshā or al-Nābighah describing a cow:

*She circled three times between day and night, and the rebuke was that she would be humbled and cry out.*

And the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*He alternates, from the prayers to the King, at times prostration, and at times crying out.*

From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out﴾ ﴿Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 64–65]. He has indicated this meaning in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is no remover of it but Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Anʿām: 17],

• and His saying: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is no remover of it but Him; and if He wills good for you, there is no repeller of His bounty; He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants﴾ to the end of the verse [Yūnus: 107],

• and His saying: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah opens for the people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him﴾ to the end of the verse [Fāṭir: 2],

• and His saying: ﴿Say: Nothing will strike us except what Allah has decreed for us; He is our Protector﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah: 51],

• and His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered what you call upon besides Allah? If Allah intends harm for me, can they remove His harm? Or if He intends mercy for me, can they withhold His mercy?﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Zumar: 38],

and other verses besides these.

It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from him (ﷺ) that he said: "O Allah, there is no preventer of what You give, no giver of what You withhold, and the fortune of the one of fortune does not benefit him against You." And in the well-known hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Know that if the whole nation gathered to benefit you, they would not benefit you except with something Allah has already written for you; and if they gathered to harm you, they would not harm you except with something Allah has already written against you. The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried."

**The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 16, verse 54:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then, when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord.﴾ In this noble verse, He, may He be exalted, explains that when harm touches the children of Adam, they call upon Allah alone, sincere to Him in religion. But when He removes the harm from them and lifts the hardship, behold, a group of them, who are the disbelievers, return as quickly as possible to what they were upon of disbelief and sins. Almighty and Exalted is He, has repeated this meaning in the Qur'an:

• As in His saying in "Yunus" (Jonah): ﴿until, when you are on the ship and they sail with them with a good wind and they rejoice in it, a violent wind comes upon it, and the waves come to them from every place, and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Yunus: 22], up to His saying: ﴿then, behold, they commit injustice on earth without right﴾ [Yunus: 23],

• And His saying in "Al-Isra'" (The Night Journey): ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you invoke vanish except Him. But when He delivers you to the land, you turn away. And mankind is ever ungrateful﴾ [Al-Isra': 67],

• And His saying at the end of "Al-'Ankabut" (The Spider): ﴿But when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 65],

• And His saying in "Al-An'am" (The Cattle): ﴿Say, "Allah delivers you from it and from every distress; then you associate others with Him"﴾ [Al-An'am: 64],

up to other verses besides these.

We have already presented this in "Surat al-An'am" in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if the punishment of Allah comes upon you..."﴾ [Al-An'am: 40].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾. The imperative form in His saying "fa-tamatta'u" [An-Nahl: 55] is for intimidation (tahdid, threat). It has been established in "the science of meanings (fann al-ma'ani), in the topic of inshā' (non-declarative speech)" and in "the science of usul (fann al-usul), in the topic of the imperative (al-amr)" that among the meanings for which the form if'al (the imperative) comes is intimidation (tahdid);

• like His saying here: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾, and other verses bear witness to this meaning;

• like His saying: ﴿Say, "Enjoy your disbelief for a little; indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire"﴾ [Az-Zumar: 8],

• and His saying: ﴿Say, "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire"﴾ [Ibrahim: 30],

• and His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; for they will soon know﴾ [Al-Hijr: 3],

• and His saying: ﴿So leave them to wade in falsehood and play until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 83; Al-Ma'arij: 42],

• and His saying: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed, you are criminals﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 46],

• and His saying: ﴿So leave them until they meet their Day in which they will be struck senseless﴾ [At-Tur: 45],

and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾ Regarding the pronoun of the subject in His saying ﴿to what they do not know﴾ [an-Nahl: 56], there are two views.

The first: it refers to the disbelievers. That is, the disbelievers assign to the idols, which they do not know that Allah commanded their worship, and do not know that they benefit their worshippers or harm their disobedient ones, a share, etc. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority and of which they have no knowledge. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ [al-Hajj: 71], and similar verses.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: The meaning of their not knowing them is:

That they name them gods, and believe in them that they harm and benefit, and intercede with Allah. But it is not so; their reality is that they are inanimate objects that neither harm nor benefit. Thus they are ignorant of them.

The second view: the waw in "yaʿlamūn" [an-Nahl: 56] refers to the idols. They are inanimate and know nothing. That is, they assign to the idols, which know nothing because they are inanimate, a share, etc. This view

- is like His saying: ﴿They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ [an-Nahl: 21],
- and His saying: ﴿So Allah is sufficient as a witness between us and you; we were certainly unaware of your worship﴾ [Yunus: 29],
- and His saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk, or hands with which they strike, or eyes with which they see?﴾ and the verse [al-A'raf: 195],

and other verses. According to this view, the waw returns to "mā" in His saying "to what they do not know," and He referred to them with "mā," which is used for non-rational beings, because those objects to which they assigned a share of the provision of Allah are inanimate and understand nothing. He used the waw in "lā yaʿlamūn" according to this view to treat the disbelievers' objects as if they were rational beings, in their claim that they intercede, harm, and benefit.

Having known this, know that this meaning mentioned in this noble verse, Allah, exalted is He, explained in (p-387) other places, such as His saying: ﴿And they assign to Allah a share of what He has produced of crops and livestock, and they say, "This is for Allah, by their claim, and this is for our partners." But what is for their partners does not reach Allah, while what is for Allah reaches their partners. Evil is what they judge.﴾ [al-An'am: 136]. That is because the disbelievers, whenever they cultivated a field or had a fruit, would assign a portion for Allah and a portion for the idol. What they assigned to the share of the idols, they guarded; and if something of what they had assigned to Allah got mixed with it, they returned it to the share of the idols; and if something of what they had assigned to Allah fell into the share of the idols, they left it there, and they said: "Allah is free of need and the idol is poor." Exalted and majestic is He, He swore that He would question them on the Day of Resurrection about this fabrication and lie, namely their claim that a share of what Allah created belongs to the idols which neither benefit nor harm, in His saying: ﴿By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate﴾ [an-Nahl: 56], and this is a questioning of rebuke and reproach.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 57:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters—glory be to Him—while for themselves is what they desire.﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given good tidings of a female, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the ill of what he has been given good tidings of. Shall he keep it in humiliation, or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they judge.﴾ His words "wa-yajʿaluna" (and they attribute) mean: they believe. In this noble verse, the Most High mentions that the disbelievers believe that Allah has female daughters. This is because the tribes of Khuza'a and Kinana used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." As He clarified with His words: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 19], so they ascribed offspring to Allah, and along with that they ascribed to Him the lowlier of the two kinds of offspring, which is the female. Thus, the females they attributed to Allah are those they themselves dislike and disdain, as He said concerning them: ﴿And when one of them is given good tidings of a female, his face becomes darkened﴾ [an-Nahl: 58], meaning that intense grief and sorrow darken the color of the face. ﴿And he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ [an-Nahl: 58], meaning: full of grief while remaining silent. It was also said: full of rage at his wife who bore him a female. ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the ill of what he has been given good tidings of﴾ [an-Nahl: 59], meaning: he hides himself from his companions because of the ill of what he has been told, lest they see what he is in of grief and sorrow, or lest they gloat over him and reproach him. He talks to himself and reflects: ﴿Shall he keep it﴾, meaning what he has been given good tidings of, which is the female, ﴿in humiliation﴾ [an-Nahl: 59], meaning in disgrace and abasement. ﴿Or bury it﴾ [an-Nahl: 59] in the dust, meaning he buries alive the one mentioned, who is the female. This refers to what they used to do to daughters of wa'd (infanticide), which is burying a girl alive, as He said: ﴿And when the buried alive girl is asked, for what sin she was killed﴾ [at-Takwir: 8–9].

The Most High clarified these meanings mentioned in these verses in other places. He explained that their assigning females to Allah, or males to themselves, is an unjust division, and that it is among the greatest falsehoods.

He also explained that if He had taken a son—exalted is He far above that!—He would have chosen the better of the two shares, and He rebuked them for ascribing to Him the lowlier of the two kinds of offspring, and He clarified their lie in that and the immensity of what they attributed to Him. He mentioned all of this in multiple places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [an-Najm: 21].

• And His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own falsehood that they say: "Allah has begotten," and indeed they are liars. Has He chosen daughters over sons? What is the matter with you, how do you judge?﴾ [as-Saffat: 151–154].

• And His saying: ﴿Has your Lord then preferred you with sons and taken for Himself females from the angels? Indeed, you say a grave saying﴾ [al-Isra': 40].

• And His saying: ﴿Or has He taken daughters from what He creates and chosen sons for you?﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 16].

• And His saying: ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills. Glory be to Him; He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [az-Zumar: 4].

• And His saying: ﴿Or for Him are daughters and for you sons?﴾ [at-Tur: 39]. The Most High also said: ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike﴾ [an-Nahl: 62]. And He said: ﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments and in disputation is not clear?﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 18]. And He said: ﴿And when one of them is given good tidings of that which he has attributed to the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 17].

He clarified the immensity of this fabrication with His saying: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ ﴿You have certainly produced something monstrous.﴾ ﴿The heavens are about to burst from it, the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ ﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ ﴿And it is not appropriate for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 88–93], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you say a grave saying﴾ [al-Isra': 40], and other verses besides these.

His saying in this verse: ﴿And for them is what they desire﴾ [an-Nahl: 57] is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). Az-Zamakhshari, al-Farra' and others mentioned that it is permissible for "ma" [an-Nahl: 59] to be in a position of accusative (nasb) by coordination with "al-banat" [an-Nahl: 57], meaning: they attribute daughters to Allah, and they attribute to themselves what they desire. az-Zajjaj cited its i'rab as accusative, and said: the Arabs use in such a context "wa-yajʿaluna li-anfusihim" (and they attribute to themselves); this is what al-Qurtubi related. Abu Hayyan said in "al-Bahr al-Muhit": az-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible for "ma" in "ma yashtahun" to be nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), and accusative on the basis that it is coordinated with "al-banat", meaning: and they assigned to themselves what they desire of males. End of quote. What he permitted regarding the accusative was followed by al-Farra' and al-Hawfi, and Abu al-Baqa', who related it, said: "In it there is consideration." These people overlooked a rule of grammar (qa'ida fi al-nahw), namely: that a verb which takes as its subject a connected pronoun does not transfer to its connected object pronoun in the accusative. Therefore it is not permissible to say: "Zayd darabahu" (Zayd struck him) meaning Zayd struck himself; except in the category of "zanna" (to think) and its sisters among the mental verbs, or verbs of loss and absence; so it is permissible to say: "Zayd zannahu qa'iman" (Zayd thought himself standing), "Zayd faqadahu" (Zayd lost himself), and "Zayd 'adimahu" (Zayd lacked himself). A pronoun governed by a preposition is like the connected accusative pronoun; so it is not permissible to say: "Zayd ghadiba 'alayhi" meaning he became angry at himself. Based on what has been established, the accusative is not permissible, since the meaning would be: "wa-yajʿaluna lahum ma yashtahun" (and they attribute to them what they desire). Thus the waw is a nominative pronoun, and "wa-lahum" (and for them) is a genitive with the preposition lam. It is like: "Zayd ghadiba 'alayhi." End of quote.

"Bishara" (good tidings) in the Arabic language is applied to news that gladdens and to news that grieves. From its application to news that grieves is his saying here: ﴿And when one of them is given good tidings of a female﴾ [an-Nahl: 58], and its parallel is His saying: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [an-Najm: 24] (or similar), and similar verses.

What the Most High mentioned in this noble verse, of their hatred of daughters, is well known and famous in their poetry. When his daughter al-Jarba' was proposed in marriage to 'Aqil ibn 'Ilfa al-Murri, he said:

Though a dowry of a thousand is brought to me, with two slaves and ten camels,
The dearest of my in-laws to me is the grave.

It is narrated for 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir his saying:

For every father of a daughter who cares for her affairs, there are three in-laws, and the in-law is praised,
A husband who cares for her, a chamber that shelters her, and a grave that conceals her—and the best of them is the grave.

They claim that the reason for their desire for their death, and their intense dislike of their birth, is fear of shame, marrying non-equals, and that their daughters be humiliated after their death. As the poet said concerning a daughter of his named Mawaddah:

Mawaddah loves the life of an old man who delights in her,
Would that death came before night, if only she knew!

He fears for her the neglect of people after him,
And no son-in-law is hoped for whom I would love more than the grave.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Allah were to seize mankind for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature﴾ [an-Nahl: 61]. In this noble verse He, may He be glorified and exalted, mentions that if He were to hasten punishment upon creation, He would destroy everyone on the earth. But He is Forbearing (ḥalīm) and does not hasten punishment, because hastening is the attribute of one who fears missing an opportunity, whereas the Lord of the heavens and the earth cannot miss anything He wills. He mentions this meaning in other places, such as His saying at the end of Surah Fāṭir: ﴿And if Allah were to seize mankind for what they have earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ [Fāṭir: 45]; and His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. If He were to seize them for what they have earned, He would have hastened punishment for them﴾ [al-Kahf: 58]. By His saying ﴿but He defers them to a specified term﴾ [an-Nahl: 61], He indicates that He gives respite and does not neglect. He clarifies this elsewhere, such as His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 42], and His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 53].

Here He clarifies that when a person's term comes, he cannot delay from it, just as he cannot advance beyond the time of his term. He explains this in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred﴾ [Nūḥ: 4], and His saying: ﴿And Allah will never defer a soul when its term has come﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 11], and other verses.

Know that His saying ﴿He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ [an-Nahl: 61] has two interpretations among the scholars:

Know that it is specific to the disbelievers, because the sin is theirs, and Allah says: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Anʿām: 164]. Those who held this view said: "creature" [an-Nahl: 61] means disbelieving creature. This view is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. It was also said that the meaning is that if He destroyed the fathers for their disbelief, the sons would not exist.

The majority of scholars, among them Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, and Abū Hurayrah, held that it is general. Another poet said:

"She loves my life and I love her death, out of compassion; and death is the most honourable guest upon the women of the household."

A Bedouin's wife gave birth to a female child, so he abandoned her out of extreme anger at her having been born a female. She said:

"What is wrong with Abū Ḥamzah that he does not come to us, / Remaining angry at the tent that is close to us? / We only bear sons, / We have no say in our affair, / We only take what we are given."

*

Notice (tanbīh).

The word "jaʿala" (جَعَلَ) comes in the Arabic language with four meanings:

The first: meaning "iʿtaqada" (to believe/consider); such as His saying here: ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters﴾ [an-Nahl: 57]. In the Khulāṣah (the versified grammar compendium) it says:

"And jaʿala is like iʿtaqada."

The second: meaning "ṣayyara" (to make/render); as already mentioned in al-Ḥijr; such as His saying: ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nūḥ: 16]. In the Khulāṣah it says:

"…and those that are like ṣayyara, and likewise, make both the subject and predicate in the accusative."

The third: meaning "khalaqa" (to create); such as His saying: ﴿All praise is for Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-Anʿām: 1], i.e., created the darknesses and the light.

The fourth: meaning "sharaʿa" (to begin/set about); such as the poet's saying:

"And I have begun, whenever I stand, that my garment weighs upon me, so I rise as the drunkard rises, intoxicated."

In the Khulāṣah it says:

"Like anshaʾa (to begin) the driver who urges on, and ṭafiqa (to start), so too jaʿaltu (I began) and akhadhtu (I took) and ʿalaqa (to begin)."

His saying in this noble verse: "Subḥānahu" [an-Nahl: 57], i.e., glorifying Him, may He be glorified and exalted, above what does not befit His perfection and majesty, namely what they attributed to Him of daughters. Glory be to Him and exalted He is far above that, with a great exaltation!

Others, as Ibn Kathīr and others transmitted from them, held that the verse is general, to the extent that the sins of the children of Adam would destroy the dung beetle in its hole and the bustard in its nest, and the like; were it not that Allah is Forbearing and does not hasten punishment, nor seize them for their wrongdoing.

The one who restricts it (muqayyiduhu), may Allah pardon him, says: This view is the correct one, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that an indefinite noun in a context of negation, when the word "min" (مِن) is added before it, becomes an explicit text in generality. Accordingly, His saying "min dābbah" (of a creature) encompasses everything that is explicitly called a dābbah.

Al-Qurṭubī said in his tafsīr: If it is asked, how can destruction encompass all when among them is a believer who is not a wrongdoer? It is answered: the destruction of the wrongdoer is made a retribution and a requital, and the destruction of the believer is compensated with the reward of the Hereafter.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When Allah intends a punishment for a people, the punishment strikes those among them, then they are resurrected according to their deeds." End of quotation, the point of which is in its wording. Hadiths of this kind are many and well known.

When it is established in the authentic hadiths that when punishment descends upon a people it encompasses the righteous and the wicked, (p-392) there is no difficulty in the destruction reaching the animals that do not reason. And when Allah intends to destroy a people, He commands their prophet and those who believe among them to leave them, because when destruction descends, it encompasses all.

*

Notice (tanbīh).

His saying: ﴿not a single creature upon it﴾ [an-Nahl: 61]. The pronoun in ʿalayhā ("upon it") refers to something not previously mentioned, namely the earth; because His saying "min dābbah" (a creature) indicates it, since it is known that creatures only crawl upon the earth. A parallel is His saying: ﴿not a single creature upon its back﴾ [Fāṭir: 45], and His saying: ﴿until it [the sun] disappeared behind the veil﴾ [Ṣād: 32], i.e., the sun, though it has not been mentioned. The return of a pronoun to something not mentioned, indicated by the context, is common in the speech of the Arabs. Among this is the saying of Ḥumayd ibn Thawr:

"And a dun-coloured she-camel from among them, like a ship, whose gestation ripened her with a load, until its count exceeded a month."

His saying "ṣahbāʾ minhā" means "of the camels," and the context "like a ship" indicates this, though the camels have not been mentioned. Also among this is the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī:

"O Umaymah, wealth does not avail a man when his breath rattles one day and the chest becomes constricted with it."

His saying "ḥashrajat wa-ḍāqa bihā" refers to the soul (nafs), which has not been mentioned; the context "wa-ḍāqa bihā al-ṣadr" indicates it. Also among this is Labīd in his Muʿallaqah:

"Until, when she [the sun] cast her hand into a disbeliever, and her darkness concealed the gaps of the frontiers."

His saying "alqat" means "the sun," which has not been mentioned; but the saying "wa-ajanna ʿawrāt al-thughūr ẓalāmuhā" indicates it. Because "alqat yadan fī kāfir" means "she entered the darkness." Also among this is Ṭarafah's saying in his Muʿallaqah:

"Upon the like of her I proceed when my companion says: 'Would that I could ransom you from her and be ransomed!'"

His saying "afdīka minhā" means "the desert" (falāh), which has not been mentioned; but the context of the speech indicates it.

His saying, in this noble verse: ﴿yuʾākhidhu﴾ [an-Nahl: 61]. Apparently the mufāʿalah form (muʾākhadhah, "to seize/take to account") here has the meaning of the bare verb: so the meaning of "ākhadha al-nās yu'ākhidhuhum" is "akhadhahum bi-dhunūbihim" (He seized them for their sins), because the mufāʿalah requires two parties. Its coming in the sense of the bare form is attested, such as: "sāfara" (to travel) and "ʿāfā" (to pardon). As for His saying "yu'ākhidhu" [an-Nahl: 61]: if we say the present tense here has the meaning of the past, there is no difficulty. If we say it has the meaning of the future, then it is the use of "law" (if) with the future, which is rare; such as His saying: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them﴾ [an-Nisāʾ: 9], and the saying of Qays ibn al-Mulawwaḥ:

"And if our echoes were to meet after our death, and beyond our two graves there were a desert plain, / The echo of my voice would remain, even if I were a decayed bone, rejoicing and delighted at the echo of Laylā's voice."

Interpreting it in the past tense in the verse is an obvious artifice, and it is absolutely impossible in the two lines of verse; and its examples are numerous in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. He indicated this in the Khulāṣah with his saying:

"Law, a conditional particle, is used with the past tense; its use with the future is rare, but it is accepted."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 62:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they assign to Allah what they dislike﴾. In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted left vague what it is that they assign to Allah and dislike, because He expressed it by the relative pronoun "mā" (what), which is an ambiguous noun, and the relative clause would not clarify the nature of this ambiguous thing beyond saying that they dislike it. However, He clarified it in other places: that it is daughters, partners, and the assigning to Him of wealth which He created for others. He said concerning daughters: ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters﴾ [an-Nahl: 57], then He clarified their dislike of them in many verses, such as His words: ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female [child]...﴾ to the end of the verse [an-Nahl: 61].

And He said concerning partners: ﴿And they have made for Allah partners﴾ to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 100], and similar verses. He clarified their dislike of partners in their provision by His words: ﴿He presents to you an example from yourselves. Do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided you so that you are equal therein, fearing them as you fear one another?  Thus do We detail the verses for a people who reason﴾ [ar-Rum: 28]. That is: if one of you does not accept that his owned slave be a partner to him, equal to himself in all that he has, then how do you make the idols partners to Allah in His worship, which is His right over His servants! He clarified their assigning to the idols some of the provision Allah created in His words: ﴿And they assign to Allah a portion of what He has created of crops and livestock﴾, up to His words: ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ [an-Nahl: 136], and His words: ﴿And they assign to what they do not know a portion of what We have provided them﴾ [an-Nahl: 56], as has preceded.

* *

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And their tongues describe the lie that for them is the best﴾. Allah the Exalted mentioned in this noble verse that the disbelievers utter with their tongues the lie; so they claim that for them is the best (al-husna). Al-husna is the feminine of al-ahsan (the best). It was said: what is meant by it is the males, as has preceded in His words: ﴿And for them is what they desire﴾ (p-394) [an-Nahl: 57]. The truth about which there is no doubt is that what is meant by al-husna is their claim that if the Hereafter is real, then they will have in it the best portion, as they had in this world. Two proofs confirm the correctness of this last view:

The first: the abundance of Qur'anic verses explaining this meaning;

• such as His words about the disbeliever: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed for me with Him is the best (al-husna)﴾ [Fussilat: 50],

• and His words: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than these as a destination﴾ [al-Kahf: 36],

• and His words: ﴿And he said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"﴾ [Maryam: 77],

• and His words: ﴿And they say, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished"﴾ [Saba': 35],

• and His words: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children is [because] We hasten to them good things?﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Mu'minun: 55],

and other verses besides these.

The second proof: Allah followed His words ﴿that for them is the best﴾ [an-Nahl: 62] with His words: ﴿Without doubt, for them is the Fire﴾ to the end of the verse [an-Nahl: 62], which clearly indicates what we have mentioned. And Allah knows best. The verbal noun formed from "anna" and its complement in His words ﴿that for them is the best﴾ [an-Nahl: 62] is in the accusative position, as a substitute (badal) for His words "al-kadhib" (the lie). The meaning of their tongues describing the lie is that their saying it is a plain statement of falsehood with no concealment.

Az-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf, in explaining Allah's words: ﴿And do not say, for what your tongues describe as falsehood﴾ [an-Nahl: 116], the following text: "If you ask: what is the meaning of their tongues describing the lie? I say: it is of eloquent and fluent speech; it makes their statement as if it were the very essence and pure substance of the lie; so when their tongues utter it, they have dressed the lie in its adornment and fashioned it in its form. Like the saying: 'Her face describes beauty, and her eye describes magic.'" End of quotation.

* *

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Without doubt, for them is the Fire, and they are neglected (mufrațūn)﴾. In this word there are two Sab'i readings and a third reading that is not Sab'i. The majority of the Seven read it: ﴿mufratūn﴾, with a sukun on the fa' and a fatha on the ra', in the form of the passive participle, from afrataho. Nafi' read it with a kasra on the ra', in the form of the active participle, from afrata. The reading that is not Sab'i is with a fatha on the fa' and a shadda-ed kasra on the ra', in the form of the active participle from farrata (the doubled form), and this reading is transmitted from Abu Ja'far. All these readings have a valid basis in the Book of Allah.

As for the reading of the majority, ﴿mufratūn﴾, in the passive form, it is a passive participle from afrataho, meaning: when he forgot it and left it, not attending to it. So His words ﴿mufratūn﴾ mean: abandoned and forgotten in the Fire. What supports this meaning is His words: ﴿Today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their day﴾ [al-A'raf: 51], His words: ﴿So taste, for what you forgot the meeting of this your day; indeed We have forgotten you, so taste the punishment of eternity﴾ to the end of the verse [as-Sajdah: 14], and His words: ﴿And it will be said, "Today We forget you as you forgot the meeting of this your day, and your refuge is the Fire"﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Jathiyah: 34]. So forgetting in these verses means abandonment in the Fire. As for forgetting in the sense of the loss of knowledge, it is impossible for Allah, as He said: ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64], and He said: ﴿He said, "Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Record; my Lord neither errs nor forgets"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52].

Among those who said that the meaning of ﴿mufratūn﴾ is forgotten and abandoned in the Fire are: Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Ibn al-A'rabi, Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Farra', and others.

Some scholars said: the meaning of His words ﴿mufratūn﴾, according to the reading of the majority, is: sent forward to the Fire, hastened. From afrattu fulanan and farratuhu in seeking water, when I sent him ahead. From this is the hadith: "I am your fara (forerunner) at the Basin," i.e., your one who goes ahead. From this is the saying of al-Qutami: "They hastened us, and they were of our companions, as a forerunner [sent] to watering-places [goes ahead]." And the saying of ash-Shanfara:

"I resolved and it resolved, so we hastened, and it poured forth; and a forerunner of mine, deliberate, turned back."

That is: one who goes ahead to the water. According to the reading of Nafi', it is an active participle from afrata fi al-amr, when one exceeds in the matter and goes beyond the limit. What supports this reading is His words: ﴿And indeed the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 43], and similar verses. According to the reading of Abu Ja'far, it is an active participle from farrata fi al-amr, when one neglects it and falls short in it. What supports this meaning is His words: ﴿Lest a soul say, "Oh, my regret over what I neglected in regard to Allah"﴾ to the end of the verse [az-Zumar: 56]. Thus you have come to know the aspects of the readings in the verse and what the Qur'an supports of them.

His words: "la jaram" (without doubt) mean: truly, that for them is the Fire. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: "la" is a rejection of their statement, and the speech is complete; i.e., it is not as you claim, and "jaram" that for them is the Fire: truly, for them is the Fire! Some scholars said: "la" is extra (silah), and "jaram" means earning; i.e., their deeds earned for them that for them is the Fire.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾. In this noble verse, He, may He be exalted and high, explains that in livestock there is a sign indicating the uniqueness of the One who created them, and who produced their milk pure from between dung and blood; that He alone deserves to be worshipped, obeyed, and not disobeyed. He also clarified this meaning in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you therein are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21].
• And His saying: ﴿And the livestock He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾ [al-Nahl: 5].
• And His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, from what Our hands have made, livestock, so they are their owners? And We subjected them to them, so some of them they ride, and some of them they eat. And for them therein are benefits and drinks; will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71-73].
• And His saying: ﴿Then do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17],
along with other verses.

The verses mentioned show that the word "livestock" (al-an'am) may be treated as masculine or feminine. He used the masculine here, in His saying: ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾ [al-Nahl: 66], and used the feminine in Surah "Qad aflaha al-mu'minun" in His saying: ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you therein are many benefits﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21]. It is known in Arabic that collective nouns (asma' al-ajnas) may be treated as masculine, looking at the wording, or feminine, looking at the meaning of the group included under the collective noun. The Qur'an has both the masculine and feminine usage of "livestock," as we have mentioned just now. It also has both usages for "palm trees": the masculine in His saying: ﴿As if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar: 20], and the feminine in His saying: ﴿As if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7], and similar. And the Qur'an has both usages for "heaven": the masculine in His saying: ﴿The heaven will be split by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18], and the feminine in His saying: ﴿And the heaven, We built it with strength﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47], and similar verses. This is well known in Arabic, and among its evidences is the saying of Qays ibn al-Husayn al-Harithi al-Asadi, while he was young, on the masculine treatment of camels (ni'am):

Every year there is a camel you keep; a people impregnate it, and you give birth to it.

And Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Shu'bah from 'Asim read this word "nusqikum" with a fatha on the nun. The rest read it with a damma, as has preceded with its evidences in Surah al-Hijr.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse:

The first issue: Al-Qadi Isma'il deduced from the masculine pronoun in His saying: ﴿from what is in their bellies﴾ [al-Nahl: 66] that the milk of the stallion establishes prohibition (of marriage). He said: it was only brought masculine because it refers to the male of the cattle, since milk is reckoned to the male, and for this reason the Prophet ﷺ ruled: "That the milk of the stallion makes unlawful," when 'A'ishah denied it in the hadith of Aflah, the brother of Abu al-Qu'ays. So for the woman there is the watering (suqya), and for the man there is the impregnating (liqah); thus the sharing of it between them occurs. End of quote. Transmitted through al-Qurtubi.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: As for considering the milk of the stallion in prohibition, there is no doubt about it, and the hadith mentioned in the story of 'A'ishah with Aflah, the brother of Abu al-Qu'ays, supports it; it is agreed upon and well known. As for deducing this from the return of the pronoun in the verse, in my view it is not free of remoteness and strain. And Allah knows best.

* *

The second issue: Al-Naqqash and others deduced from this noble verse that semen is not impure. They said: just as milk comes out from between dung and blood, pure and unmixed, palatable, so it is permissible for semen to come out from the urinary passage pure.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is indeed a great ignorance and a shameful deduction. The report about milk came as a blessing and favor issuing from power, so that it would be a lesson; all of that requires the description of purity and pleasantness. Semen is not in this state, so that it could be attached to it or analogized with it.

Al-Qurtubi said after quoting the above words: I say: this may be countered by saying: what is greater and more exalted than the emission of semen from which a noble human being comes into being? Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿It comes out from between the loins and the ribs﴾ [al-Tariq: 7], and He said: ﴿And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves, and made for you from your spouses sons and grandsons﴾ [al-Nahl: 72], and this is the utmost in favor.

If it is said: it becomes impure by its emission through the urinary passage.

We say: That is what we meant; the impurity is accidental and its origin is pure. End of the relevant point from al-Qurtubi's words.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: Deriving the ruling on the purity of semen from this noble verse, in my view, is not free of remoteness. We will explain, if Allah wills, the ruling on semen: whether it is impure or pure, and the views of the scholars on that, along with discussion of the evidences. Know that regarding human semen there are three views among the scholars:

The first: that it is pure, and its ruling is that of mucus and phlegm. This is the school of al-Shafi'i, and the more correct of the two narrations from Ahmad. It was also said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata', Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Abu Thawr, Dawud, and Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-'Abdari and others related it from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn 'Umar, and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them, as al-Nawawi transmitted it in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab and elsewhere.

The second view: that it is impure, and its purification necessarily requires water, whether it is dry or wet. This is the school of Malik, al-Thawri, and al-Awza'i.

The third view: that it is impure; wet semen necessarily requires water, but dry semen does not need water, rather it is purified by rubbing it off the garment until it is removed from it. This is the school of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shawkani in Nayl al-Awtar chose that it is impure, and that its removal does not depend on water absolutely.

As for the argument of those who say it is pure like what is mixed, it is by both text and analogy. It is known in the principles that analogy agreeing with a text is not objectionable, since it is another supporting evidence for the text, and there is no objection to the agreement of evidences.

As for the text, it is what is established from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I used to rub the semen off the garment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then he would go and pray in it." Muslim recorded it in his Sahih, and the authors of the four Sunan and Imam Ahmad. They said: her rubbing it while it is dry, and his praying in the garment without mention of washing, is evidence of purity. In a narration with Ahmad: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to scrape the semen from his garment with a sprig of idhkhir, then pray in it, and rub it from his garment when dry, then pray in it. In another narration, from 'A'ishah in al-Daraqutni: "I used to rub the semen from the garment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when it was dry, and wash it when it was wet." And from Ishaq ibn Yusuf, who said: Sharik narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ was asked about semen that gets on a garment, so he said: ''It is merely like mucus and spittle, and it is enough for you to wipe it with a rag or a sprig of idhkhir.''"

The author of Muntaqa al-Akhbar, after quoting this hadith as we have mentioned, said: al-Daraqutni narrated it and said: No one raised it except Ishaq al-Azraq from Sharik. I say: This does not harm, since Ishaq is an imam from whom both Sahihs narrate, so his raising and his addition are accepted.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: What the eminent imam (al-Majd) said in al-Muntaqa about accepting the raising and addition of a trustworthy narrator is the correct view among the people of principles and the people of hadith, as we have explained many times, along with other hadiths about rubbing semen and not being ordered to wash it.

As for the analogy supporting the text, it is from two aspects. One of them: attaching semen to eggs, by the common cause that each of them is a fluid from which a living pure animal is formed, and eggs are pure by consensus; so it follows that semen is pure too.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: This type of analogy is known as formal analogy (al-qiyas al-suwari). Most scholars do not accept it, and only Isma'il ibn 'Ulayyah became known for holding it, as indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud in his saying:

And Ibn 'Ulayyah sees the formal analogy as the mule is to horses over donkeys.

There are many disputed instances of formal analogy, such as analogizing horses to donkeys regarding the falling away of zakat and the prohibition of eating, due to formal resemblance; and analogizing semen to eggs for the generation of a pure animal from each of them in purity; and analogizing one of the two tashahhuds to the other regarding obligation or recommendation, due to their similarity in form; and analogizing the first sitting to the second regarding obligation, due to its resembling it in form; and attaching the wild cat to the domestic cat regarding prohibition; and attaching sea pig and sea dog to land pig and land dog, along with other of its many well-known forms in the principles. Those who hold formal analogy argue: that the texts indicate the consideration of formal resemblance in rulings, such as His saying: ﴿Then the compensation is like what he killed of the livestock﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], where the intended meaning, according to the majority, is resemblance in form. And like the substitute of a loan, which is returned in like form. The Prophet ﷺ borrowed a young camel and returned a four-year-old, as is established in the Sahih. And they cite the Prophet's ﷺ approval of the words of the physiognomist (al-qa'if) al-Mudlaji concerning Zayd ibn Harithah and his son Usamah: "These feet are some of them from others," because physiognomy is formal analogy, since the physiognomist relies on resemblance in form.

The second aspect of the mentioned analogy: attaching semen to clay, by the common cause that each of them is the beginning of the creation of a human being, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed We created man from an extract of clay. Then We made him a drop (nutfah)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12-13].

If it is said: this analogy necessitates the purity of the clot ('alaqah), which is congealed blood, since it too is the beginning of human creation, due to His saying: ﴿Then We made the drop a clot﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], and blood is impure without disagreement.

The answer: analogizing blood to clay in purity is invalid in consideration, due to the existence of a text on the impurity of blood. As for analogizing semen to clay, it is not invalid in consideration, since no text on the impurity of semen has come.

(p-400) As for the argument of those who say that semen is impure, it is by both text and analogy as well. As for the text, it is what is established from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I used to wash the semen from the garment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then he would go out to prayer while the trace of the washing was on his garment as spots of water," agreed upon. They said: her washing it is evidence that it is impure. In a narration in Muslim from 'A'ishah with the wording: "That the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to wash the semen, then go out to prayer in that garment while I was looking at the trace of the washing in it."

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: This narration established in the Sahih of Muslim strengthens the argument of those who say it is impure, since what is established in the principles is that the present-tense verb after the word "kana" (was) indicates constancy in that action. So 'A'ishah's saying in this narration of Muslim: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to wash," indicates the frequency of that occurrence from him and his constancy in it, and this indicates the necessity of washing. And in another narration from 'A'ishah in the Sahih of Muslim as well: "That a man stayed with her and in the morning washed his garment. 'A'ishah said: It would have sufficed you, if you saw it, to wash its place. If you did not see it, sprinkle around it. And indeed I used to rub it from the garment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with rubbing, and he would pray in it." End of quote.

They said: this narration established in the Sahih from 'A'ishah explicitly states that it is sufficient to wash its place. It is established in the principles (in the topic of the indication of the discourse, dalil al-khitab) and in the rhetorical sciences (in the topic of restriction, al-qasr) that "innama" is one of the particles of restriction. So 'A'ishah explicitly restricted sufficiency to washing; this indicates that rubbing alone does not suffice without washing. And there are other hadiths indicating its washing.

al-Shinqiti's argument from analogy: "As for analogy, their analogy of semen to urine and menstrual blood. They said: Also, because it exits from the place of urine, and because madhy is a part of semen, since desire dissolves each of them, so they share in impurity."

"As for the evidence of the one who said that it is impure, and that its dry form is purified by rubbing and does not need washing, it is the apparent meaning of texts which indicate this. Among the clearest of them in this is the hadith of 'Aisha in al-Daraqutni, which we presented just before: 'I used to rub the semen from the garment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when it was dry, and I would wash it when it was wet.'"

Al-Mujidd said in Muntaqa al-Akhbar, after he narrated this report, the following: "I say: it has become clear from the totality of the texts that both are permissible."

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, said: The explanation of the inference from this hadith for this view is that the eagerness (p-401) to remove the semen entirely is evidence of its impurity, and the sufficiency of rubbing for its dry form indicates that it does not need water. There is nothing strange about an impure thing being purified by other than water; for impurities on shoes and sandals whose impurity is agreed upon are purified by rubbing until their substance is removed. Of this kind is the statement of al-Shawkani: that it is purified absolutely by removal without washing, because of what came in some reports about wiping its wet form with an idhkhira (a fragrant reed) or the like. Those who said that semen is pure rejected the argument of those who held it impure, saying: washing does not indicate that something is impure, so there is no necessary link between washing and making impure, since it is permissible to wash pure things such as dust and mud that reach the body or garment. They said: no report has been established about a command to wash it, and the bare act does not indicate anything beyond permissibility.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis: A command to rub it has come through a sound route, narrated by Ibn al-Jarud: in al-Muntaqa, from Muhsin ibn Yahya, from Abu Hudhayfa, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, from Hammam ibn al-Harith, who said: a guest was with 'Aisha and he became junub, so he began washing what had touched him; 'Aisha said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to command us to scrape it off... until he said: As for the command to wash it, it has no basis.

They answered 'Aisha's statement, "It is sufficient for you only to wash its place," by understanding it as recommended, because she argued by rubbing. They said: if washing were obligatory, her words would be a proof against her, not for her; she only intended to object to washing the whole garment, so she said: "Washing the whole garment is a reprehensible innovation, and it suffices you, for attaining the better and more complete, to wash its place..." etc.

They answered the analogy of semen to urine and blood: semen is the origin of the honoured human being, so it resembles clay more, unlike urine and blood.

They answered the claim that it exits from the place of urine by denial. They said: rather, their exits differ, and the penis of a man among the Romans was split, and it was found to be so, so we do not make it impure on doubt. They said: even if it were established that it exits from the place of urine, impurity would not necessarily follow from that, because contact with impurity in the interior does not have effect; only contact on the exterior has effect.

They also answered the claim that madhy is a part of semen by denial as well. They said: rather, it differs from it in name, form, and manner of exit; for the self and the penis become languid by the exit of semen, whereas with madhy it is the reverse, and that is why one who has continuous madhy-flow does not emit anything of semen. There are many disputes among the scholars about this issue, many of which are of no benefit. What we have mentioned here is the essence of the views of the scholars (p-402) and their proofs.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, said: The view with the strongest evidence in this question in my opinion, and Allah knows best, is that semen is pure, because of the hadith of Ishaq al-Azraq which we presented earlier, from Sharik, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "It is only like mucus and spittle, and it suffices you to wipe it with a cloth or an idhkhira." This is an explicit text on the point in dispute.

We have previously quoted from the author of al-Muntaqa that al-Daraqutni said: none raised it except Ishaq al-Azraq from Sharik; and that he himself said: I say: this does not harm, because Ishaq is an imam whose narrations are included in the Two Sahihs, so his raising and addition are accepted. End of quote.

We have also said many times that this is the truth: if a hadith comes as mawquf through one route and as marfu' through another sound route, it is judged as marfu', because raising is an addition, and additions by trustworthy narrators are accepted. Said in Maraqi al-Su'ud:

"Raising, connecting, and an added wording are accepted by the imam of memorization."

...etc.

By this you know the soundness of arguing with the aforementioned marfu' report of Ishaq, especially since it has a witness through another route.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis, verbatim: Benefit: al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi narrated through the route of Ishaq al-Azraq, from Sharik, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ was asked about semen that touches a garment. He said: 'It is only like mucus and spittle,'" and he said: "It is sufficient for you to wipe it with a cloth or an idhkhira." Al-Tahawi narrated it from the hadith of Habib ibn Abi 'Amra, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, marfu'; he and al-Bayhaqi narrated it through the route of 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, mawquf. Al-Bayhaqi said: the mawquf is the sound one. End of quote.

So I have seen the other marfu' route from the hadith of Habib ibn Abi 'Amra, from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, and it strengthens the route of Ishaq al-Azraq mentioned earlier.

Know that al-Bayhaqi's statement, may Allah have mercy on him, "the mawquf is the sound one," does not nullify the argument from the marfu' report; for he holds that stopping the hadith on that route is a defect in the marfu' route. This is a known view of some scholars of hadith and principles, but the truth is that raising (p-403) is an accepted addition from a trustworthy narrator. By this you know the soundness of arguing with the marfu' report from Ibn 'Abbas on the purity of semen, and it is an explicit text on the point in dispute. Nothing in the texts of the Sharia explicitly states that semen is impure.

If it is said: al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili in their Musnads, Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil, al-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi and al-'Uqayli in al-Du'afa', and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifa narrated from the hadith of 'Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Prophet ﷺ passed by 'Ammar and mentioned an account, in which: "You only wash your garment from excrement, urine, semen, blood, and vomit, O 'Ammar. Your nasal mucus, the tears of your eyes, and the water in your vessel are all equal."

The answer: its chain includes Thabit ibn Hammad, from Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, and all the named scholars weakened him except Abu Ya'la; and some accused him of fabrication. Al-Lalika'i said: they agreed to abandon his hadith. Al-Bazzar said: we know of no hadith for Thabit except this one. Al-Tabarani said: Thabit ibn Hammad alone narrated it, and it is not narrated from 'Ammar except through this chain. Al-Bayhaqi said: this is a false hadith; it was narrated only by Thabit ibn Hammad, who is accused of fabrication. Said by Ibn Hajar in al-Talkhis; then he said: I say: al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani also narrated it through the route of Ibrahim ibn Zakariyya al-'Ijli, from Hammad ibn Salama, from Ali ibn Zayd, but Ibrahim is weak, and he was mistaken in it; it is narrated only by Thabit ibn Hammad. End of quote.

By this you know that this hadith cannot be validly used as evidence for the impurity of semen. And knowledge is with Allah, Exalted.

* *

The third issue: al-Qurtubi said: In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of benefiting from milk for drinking and other uses. As for the milk of a dead animal, it is not permissible to benefit from it, because it is a pure liquid that came into an impure vessel. For the udder of a dead animal is impure, while the milk is pure; when it is milked, it has been taken from an impure vessel. As for the milk of a dead woman, our companions have differed about it. Whoever said that a human is pure alive and dead holds it pure. Whoever said it becomes impure by death holds it impure. On both views the prohibition is established, because the infant may be nourished by it just as one is nourished by a living animal. For the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Suckling is that which makes flesh grow and bones rise," and he did not specify. End of al-Qurtubi's words.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 67 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 404] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes you take from them intoxicant and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]. The majority of scholars hold that what is meant by *sakar* (intoxicant) in this noble verse is *khamr* (wine). This is because the Arabs use the name *sakar* for that which produces intoxication, by way of using the verbal noun (*masdar*) to mean the concrete noun (*ism*). The Arabs say: *sikr* (with a kasra) *sakaran* (﴿sakaran﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]), *sakar* (with two fathas) and *sukran* (with a damma followed by a sukun).

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "*Al-sakar* is wine. It is named by the verbal noun of *sakara*, *sukran* and *sakaran*, like *rashida rushdan* and *rashadan*." He said:

*"They came to us with sakar against us, so the sober one today has been made clear, and the drunkard is sober."*

End quote.

And from the use of *sakar* for wine is the saying of the poet:

*"Evil are the sober, and evil is their drinking, when the mu'zar and the sakar flow among them."*

Among those who said that *sakar* in the verse means wine are: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Kalbi, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Thawr, and others. It has also been said that *sakar* means vinegar (*khall*), or food (*ta'm*), or sweet juice (*'asir*).

Since you have come to know that the sound position is the view of the majority, and that Allah bestowed this favour upon this nation by means of wine before its prohibition, know that this verse is Meccan. After it were revealed Medinan verses which explained the prohibition of wine. There are three such verses, which came after this verse that indicates the permissibility of wine:

The first: the verse of al-Baqarah, in which some of its harms and corruptions are mentioned, but its prohibition is not definitively stated. It is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. After its revelation, some people abandoned it because of the sin in it, and others drank it for the benefits in it.

The second: the verse of al-Nisa' which indicates its prohibition during the times of the prayers, but not at the times when the drinker becomes sober before the time of prayer, such as between the 'Isha' prayer and the Fajr prayer, and between the Fajr prayer and the Dhuhr prayer. It is His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43].

The third: the verse of al-Ma'idah which indicates its definitive prohibition. It is His saying: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine, gambling, stone altars and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may succeed﴾, up to His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90-91].

[p. 405] This noble verse indicates the prohibition of wine in the most complete and clearest manner, because He, may He be exalted, declared that it is an abomination (*rijs*), that it is from the work of Satan, and He commanded avoiding it with a decisive command in His saying: ﴿So avoid it﴾. Avoiding a thing (*ijtinab*) is to keep far from it, by being on a side other than the side on which it is. He linked the hope of success to avoiding it in His saying: ﴿that you may succeed﴾, and it is understood from this that whoever does not avoid it will not succeed, and this is so.

Then He explained some of its corruptions by His saying: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. Then He emphasised the prohibition by presenting it in the form of a question in His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. This is more forceful in deterrence than the imperative form, which would be *intahu* ("desist!"). It has been established in the science of *ma'ani* (rhetorical meanings) that among the meanings of the interrogative form that it may carry is the command, as in His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, and His saying: ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: Have you submitted?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20], meaning: submit!

The prepositional phrase in His saying: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms﴾ [al-Nahl: 67] is related to ﴿you take﴾, and He repeated the word *min* ("from") for emphasis. He used the singular pronoun in His saying *minhu* ("from it") in consideration of what was mentioned, meaning: you take from it, that is, from what was mentioned, the fruits of the date palms and grapes. A parallel to this is the saying of Ru'bah:

*"In it are lines of black and white, as if on the skin is the spotting of leprosy."*

So His saying "as if" refers to what was mentioned of the lines of black and white. It has been said that the pronoun refers to an omitted antecedent that the context indicates, meaning: and from the juice of the fruits of the date palms and grapes you take from it, that is, the juice of the mentioned fruits. It has been said: His saying ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿from what is in their bellies﴾ [al-Nahl: 66], meaning: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies and from the fruits of the date palms. It has been said: it is related to ﴿We give you to drink﴾ [al-Nahl: 66], with an omitted verb indicated by the first; so this is coordination of clauses. According to the first view, this is coordination of single words when they share the same governing element. It has been said: it is coordinated with "the cattle" [al-Nahl: 66], and this is the weakest of them in my view.

Al-Tabari said: The estimated construction is: "And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes, that which you take from it intoxicant," so he omitted *ma* ("that which").

Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr) said: This is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans. It has also been said: it may be an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning: and from the fruits of the date palms and grapes there is a fruit from which you take [intoxicant] (p. 406).

Of the Arabs' speech similar to this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*"You have with me nothing but a whip and a stone, and not a bow of stiff string that was given by the hands of a man who was among the best archers of mankind."*

That is: by the hands of a man who was... [etc.]. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan mentioned this.

The author of this work, may Allah pardon him, said: The most apparent of these views to me is that His saying ﴿And from the fruits of﴾ is related to ﴿you take﴾, meaning: you take from the fruits of the date palms, and that the second *min* is an emphasis of the first. The pronoun in His saying *minhu* refers to the genus of fruit understood from mentioning the fruits. And Allah knows best.

\* \*

**A note.** Know that the verified position according to the majority is that this noble verse, which is His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes﴾ [al-Nahl: 67], has been abrogated (*mansukhah*) by the mentioned verse of al-Ma'idah. What the author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud* asserted about this, both in it and in its commentary (*Nashr al-Bunud*), that the prohibition of wine is not an abrogation of its original permissibility, on the basis that its first permissibility was rational permissibility (*ibahah 'aqliyyah*), and rational permissibility is the original absence of obligation (*al-bara'ah al-asliyyah*), which is itself the presumption of the original non-existence (*istishab al-'adam al-asli*), and which is not among the legal rulings (*al-ahkam al-shar'iyyah*), so lifting it is not abrogation. He explained in *al-Maraqi* that it is not among the legal rulings in his saying:

*"What has been taken from the original absence of obligation is not legislated."*

He also said regarding the permissibility of wine before its prohibition:

*"It was permitted at the beginning of Islam by an absence of obligation which is not among the legal rulings."*

All of this is not apparent; rather it is incorrect, because the permissibility of wine before its prohibition is indicated by this noble verse, which is His saying: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes you take from it intoxicant﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]. And what a verse of the Book of Allah indicates as permissible cannot properly be said to be rational permissibility; rather it is a legislated permissibility stated in the Book of Allah, so lifting it is abrogation. Yes! According to the view that the meaning of *sakar* in the verse is vinegar, or food, or juice, then the prohibition of wine is not an abrogation of its permissibility, and its first permissibility is rational. We have explained this topic in our book (*Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab*) [p. 407].

If it is said: the verse comes in the form of a report (*khabar*), and reports do not admit abrogation, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence:

The answer: abrogation applies to what is understood from the verse of the permissibility of wine. Permissibility is a legal ruling like the rest of the rulings, capable of abrogation. So abrogation does not apply to the report itself, but to the permissibility understood from the report, as Ibn al-'Arabi al-Maliki and others verified.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67], meaning: the dates, the fresh dates, the grapes, the raisins, the juice, and the like.

**Another note.** Know that the intoxicating beverage *nabidh* of which a large quantity intoxicates may not be drunk in a small quantity that does not intoxicate because of its smallness. This is beyond doubt.

Whoever claims the permissibility of drinking a small quantity that does not intoxicate, such as the Hanafiyyah and others, has erred a gross error; because that of which a large quantity intoxicates is, by the indication of the literal denotation (*dalalat al-mutabaqah*), truly described as intoxicating, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is forbidden." And it is authentically established from him (ﷺ) in the Sahih that he said: "Every intoxicant is wine, and every wine is forbidden." If the opponent were to dispute the meaning of these hadiths, claiming that the small quantity that does not intoxicate is no longer called intoxicating, so its prohibition does not follow, we say: He (ﷺ) declared that "what a large quantity of it intoxicates, its small quantity is forbidden," and this is a clear text on the point in dispute, with which no argument can stand. From 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with him, she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is forbidden, and what the *faraq* intoxicates, a handful of it is forbidden." It was related by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and al-Tirmidhi, who said: a good hadith. From Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "What a large quantity of it intoxicates, its small quantity is forbidden." It was related by Ahmad, Ibn Majah, and al-Daraqutni, who authenticated it. Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, and al-Tirmidhi have a similar report, exactly the same, from the hadith of Jabir. Likewise Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah have it from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather. Likewise al-Daraqutni has it from the hadith of the Imam 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. From Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: that the Prophet (ﷺ) "forbade the small quantity of what its large quantity intoxicates," related by al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni. From 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: that the Prophet (ﷺ) was approached by a people who said: "O Messenger of Allah, we steep the *nabidh* and drink it with our lunch and our dinner?" He said: "Drink, for every intoxicant is forbidden." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we dilute it with water?" [p. 408] He said: "Forbidden is the small quantity of what its large quantity intoxicates." Related by al-Daraqutni. End quote, through the transmission of al-Majd in *Muntaqa al-Akhbar*.

These hadiths leave no ambiguity regarding the prohibition of a small quantity of what a large quantity intoxicates. Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari*, in explaining his saying (ﷺ) recorded by al-Bukhari: "Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden," the following text: In Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, and authenticated by Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of Jabir, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What a large quantity of it intoxicates, its small quantity is forbidden." And in al-Nasa'i, from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, the like of it, and its chain to 'Amr is sound. In Abu Dawud, from the hadith of 'A'ishah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every intoxicant is forbidden, and what the *faraq* of it intoxicates, a handful of it is forbidden." In Ibn Hibban and al-Tahawi, from the hadith of 'Amir ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I forbid you the small quantity of what its large quantity intoxicates." Al-Tahawi acknowledged the soundness of these hadiths, and said: It has also come from 'Ali in al-Daraqutni, from Ibn 'Umar in Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabarani, from Khawwat ibn Jubayr in al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Tabarani, and from Zayd ibn Thabit in al-Daraqutni. There is discussion regarding their chains, but they add strength and fame to the hadiths that precede them.

Abu al-Muzaffar ibn al-Sam'ani (who was a Hanafi, then converted to Shafi'i) said: The reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the prohibition of intoxicants are firmly established.

Then he cited many of them, and then said: The reports on this matter are numerous, and there is no room for anyone to deviate from them or to speak against them, for they are decisive proofs. He said: The Kufans have erred in this matter; they narrated on it reports that are defective (mu'allal), which cannot in any way counter these reports. Whoever thinks that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drank an intoxicant has entered into a grave matter and incurred a great sin. What he drank was sweet and was not intoxicating. Thumamah ibn Hazn al-Qushayri narrated: that he asked 'A'ishah about nabidh, and she summoned an Abyssinian slave-girl and said: Ask her, for she used to prepare nabidh for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Abyssinian woman said: I used to make nabidh for him in a waterskin at night, and I would tie its mouth and hang it up, and when he rose in the morning he drank from it. Related by Muslim.
Al-Hasan al-Basri narrated from his mother from 'A'ishah something similar. Then he said: The analogy of nabidh to khamr by the effective cause of intoxication and agitation is among the most noble and clearest of analogies, and the harms found in khamr are found in nabidh... to where he said: In sum, the texts explicitly prohibiting every intoxicant, whether little or much, render analogy unnecessary. And Allah knows best.
ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: Nothing is authentically transmitted from the Companions or from the Successors permitting nabidh whose large quantity intoxicates, except from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. End of the relevant point from (Fath al-Bari), with what is unnecessary omitted.
Its annotator (may Allah forgive him) said: The prohibition of a small quantity of nabidh whose large quantity intoxicates is beyond doubt, because of what I have seen of the Prophet's (ﷺ) explicit statement: "Whatever its large quantity intoxicates, its small quantity is forbidden."
Know that the analogy of intoxicating nabidh, whose large quantity intoxicates, to khamr by the common cause of intoxication is not valid, because the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly stated that "every intoxicant is forbidden," and analogy requires that the ruling of the branch not be explicitly stated as the ruling of the root. As indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud by his saying:
"Wherever two rulings are included in the text, then say: the two matters are alike."
Ibn al-Mundhir said: The people of Kufa brought defective reports, and when people differ on a matter it is obligatory to refer it back to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). Ended.
