It also contains the beginning of the creation of man until his death, the manner of death, the seizing of the soul and what is done with it after its ascent to the heaven, the opening of the gate for the believing [soul] and the casting down of the disbelieving [soul], the punishment of the grave and the questioning in it, the abode of the spirits, and the ten major signs of the Hour, which are:

the descent of 'Isa, the emergence of the Dajjal, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the Beast, the smoke, the lifting of the Qur'an, the rising of the sun from its west, the closing of the door of repentance, and the sinking of the earth.

And the states of resurrection: from the blowing of the Trumpet, the terror, the swooning, the standing, the gathering and the dispersal, the horrors of the Place of Standing, the intensity of the heat of the sun, the shade of the Throne, the Sirat, the Scale, the Basin, the reckoning of some people and the salvation of others from it, the testimony of the limbs, the giving of the books in the right hand, the left hand and behind the backs, the intercession, the Garden and its gates, what is in it of trees, fruits, rivers, ornaments and colours, the ranks, the vision of Him, the Exalted, and the Fire and what is in it of valleys, kinds of punishment, varieties of torment, the Zaqqum and the Hamim, and beyond that of what, if it were spread out, would fill volumes.

The Qur'an contains all of Allah's beautiful names, as has been related in a hadith. It contains of His names in general a thousand names, and it contains a number of the names of the Prophet ﷺ.

It contains the branches of faith, which are seventy-some. It contains the legislations of Islam, which are three hundred and fifteen. It contains the types of major sins and many minor sins. It contains the confirmation of every hadith reported from the Prophet ﷺ. This is the sum of what is said on that. The words of al-Suyuti in (al-Iklil) have ended.

We have quoted it in full, despite its length, because of what it makes clear: that the Qur'an contains the explanation of everything. Although in the aforementioned statement there are things deserving of criticism, we have left discussing them for fear of a tedious lengthening, given the great benefit of the aforementioned statement overall.

In His exalted saying ﴿an explanation for everything﴾ [al-Nahl: 89] there are two grammatical analyses (*wujuh min al-i'rab*):

The first: that it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlih*). The second: that it is an indefinite verbal noun (*masdar munakkar*) functioning as a circumstantial state (*hal*), following the rule in his words in *al-Khulasa* (the Alfiyya summary of Ibn Malik):

*"And an indefinite verbal noun comes as a state, frequently, like 'baghtatan' (suddenly) — Zayd arrived."*

Note (*tanbih*):

The more apparent of the two opinions is that *tibyan* is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the pattern *tifal* with a kasra on the first letter has not been heard as a verbal noun except in *tibyan* and *tilqa'*. Some scholars said: *tibyan* is a noun (*ism*), not a verbal noun. Abu Hayyan said in (al-Bahr): The apparent view is that "*tibyanan*" is a verbal noun that came on the pattern *tif'al*, although the general pattern of verbal nouns comes on *taf'al* with a fatha, like *tardad* and *tawaf*. The analogue of *tibyan* in the kasra of its *ta'* is *tilqa'*, and al-Zajjaj permitted its fatha outside the Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Tibyanan*" is a noun, not a verbal noun, and this is the view of most grammarians. Tha'lab related from the Kufans, and al-Mubarrad from the Basrans, that it is a verbal noun, and that no verbal noun came on *tif'al* except two forms: *tibyan* and *tilqa'*. End of quotation. And Allah knows best.

* *

His exalted saying: ﴿And a guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims﴾. In this noble verse, He, Majestic and Exalted, mentions that this great Qur'an is guidance, mercy and good tidings for the Muslims. From the implication of this noble verse (*mafhum al-mukhalafa*, the implication of contrast) it is understood that non-Muslims are not so. This implication from this verse He, Majestic and Exalted, has stated explicitly in other places:

• Like His saying: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is for them blindness﴾ [Fussilat: 44];

• And His saying: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers, but it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra': 82];

• And His saying, Majestic and Exalted: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, among them are those who say: "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. And as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has increased them in filth upon their filth, and they died while they were disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124–125];

• And His saying: ﴿And surely many of them will increase in transgression and disbelief by what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64],

in both places.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 90:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that you may remember﴾. In this noble verse He, may He be exalted and high, mentions that He orders His creation to be just and to do good, and to give to relatives, and that He forbids them from immorality, bad conduct and oppression, so that they may be admonished by His commands and prohibitions, comply with His command, and avoid His prohibition. The object of "yaʾmuru" (orders) and "yanhā" (forbids) is omitted for the purpose of generality.

Among the verses in which He commanded justice is His saying: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent is that which Allah instructs you﴾ [an-Nisa': 58].

Among the verses in which He commanded good conduct (iḥsān) is His saying: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands. And do good; indeed, Allah loves the doers of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], and His saying: ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Isra': 23], and His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 77], and His saying: ﴿And speak to people good words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the doers of good﴾ [at-Tawbah: 91].

Among the verses in which He commanded giving to relatives is His saying: ﴿So give the relative his right, and the needy and the traveler﴾ [ar-Rum: 38], and His saying: ﴿And give the relative his right, and the needy and the traveler, and do not spend wastefully﴾ [al-Isra': 26], and His saying: ﴿And gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives﴾ — the verse [al-Baqarah: 177], and His saying: ﴿Or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan of near relation﴾ [al-Balad: 14–15], along with other verses.

Among the verses in which He forbade immorality, bad conduct and oppression is His saying: ﴿And do not approach immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾ — the verse [al-An'am: 151], and His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin and oppression without right﴾ — the verse [al-A'raf: 33], and His saying: ﴿And leave the outward and inward of sin. Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they have been committing﴾ [al-An'am: 120]. Although bad conduct (al-munkar) is not named explicitly in these verses, it is included within them.

Among the verses in which He combined the command to justice with the favour of good conduct is His saying: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾ [an-Nahl: 126]; this is justice. Then He called to good conduct by His saying: ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ [an-Nahl: 126]. And His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [ash-Shura: 40]; this is justice. Then He called to good conduct by His saying: ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [ash-Shura: 40].

And His saying: ﴿And wounds are subject to retribution﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]; this is justice. Then He called to good conduct by His saying: ﴿But whoever gives it as charity, it is an expiation for him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. And His saying: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those — there is no path [of blame] against them﴾ — the verse [ash-Shura: 41], this is justice. Then He called to good conduct by His saying: ﴿But whoever is patient and forgives, indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [ash-Shura: 43]. And His saying: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾ [an-Nisa': 148]; this is justice. Then He called to good conduct by His saying: ﴿Whether you disclose a good or conceal it or pardon an evil, indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ [an-Nisa': 149], along with other verses.

When you have understood this, know that justice ('adl) in the language means equity, fairness, and absence of injustice. Its origin is moderation between two extremes, namely excess (ifrāṭ) and deficiency (tafrīṭ). Whoever avoids both excess and deficiency has been just. Iḥsān is the verbal noun of aḥsana, and it is used transitively with a preposition, as in: "Be good to your parents." From this is His saying, may He be exalted, concerning Yusuf: ﴿And he was certainly good to me when he took me out of prison﴾ — the verse [Yusuf: 100]. It is also used transitively without a preposition, as in your saying: "The worker did his work well," meaning he perfected it and brought it out good. Allah, may He be exalted and high, orders iḥsān in both of its senses that have been mentioned, and both are included in the noble verse, because doing good to the servants of Allah for the sake of Allah is an action in which its doer has done well. The Prophet ﷺ explained iḥsān in the hadith of Jibril by his saying: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." We have previously clarified this in (Surah Hud).

When you have understood this, know that the sayings of the commentators on the noble verse generally return to what we have mentioned. Such is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "Justice is: there is no god but Allah; and good conduct is: performing the obligations." Because worshipping the Creator alone, and not the created, is the very essence of fairness and equity, and avoiding deficiency and excess. Whoever performs the obligations of Allah in the most complete manner has done good; therefore the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the man who swore that he would not add to the obligatory duties: "He has succeeded if he is truthful." Such also is the saying of Sufyan: "Justice is the evenness of the outward and the inward. And good conduct is that the inward be better than the outward." Such also is the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Justice is fairness. And good conduct is generosity." And besides these, there are other sayings of the early generations (salaf). And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted. As for His saying: ﴿He admonishes you that you may remember﴾ [an-Nahl: 90], al-wa'ẓ (admonition) is speech by which hearts are softened.

A Caution.

If it is said: In the Qur'an the term "admonition" is frequently applied to commands and prohibitions;

• As in His saying here: ﴿He admonishes you that you may remember﴾ [an-Nahl: 90], although He mentioned only the command and the prohibition in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah orders justice…﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and forbids immorality﴾ — the verse [an-Nahl: 90];

• And as in His saying in (Surah al-Baqarah), after mentioning the rulings of divorce and reconciliation: ﴿With this is admonished whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 232];

• And His saying (concerning divorce) in a similar manner also: ﴿That is admonished by it whoever was among you believing in Allah and the Last Day﴾;

• And His saying concerning the prohibition of the like of the slander of 'A'ishah: ﴿Allah admonishes you never to repeat the like of it, ever﴾ — the verse [an-Nur: 17];

while it is well known among people that admonition occurs through encouragement and warning and the like, not through command and prohibition.

The answer: The criterion of admonition is speech by which hearts are softened, and what softens the hearts of the intelligent most is the commands and prohibitions of their Lord. For when they hear a command, they fear the wrath of Allah for not complying with it, and they hope for the reward of Allah for complying with it. And when they hear a prohibition, they fear the wrath of Allah for not avoiding it, and they hope for the reward He has for avoiding it. Thus the driver of fear and hope urges them to compliance, and their hearts become soft to obedience out of fear and hope. In the language of the Arabs, al-fāḥishah (immorality) is the characteristic that is extreme in ugliness. From this it is said of one who is extremely stingy: fāḥish, as in the saying of Tarafa in his Mu'allaqah:

"I see death choosing the noble, and selecting
the precious wealth of the miserly, harsh one."

Al-munkar is the passive participle of ankara, and in the Shari'ah it is what the Shari'ah has disapproved and forbidden, and for whose doer it has threatened punishment. Al-baghy is oppression.

Allah, may He be exalted, has made clear that the harm of the oppressor returns upon himself, in His saying: ﴿O mankind, your oppression is only against yourselves﴾ [Yunus: 23],

• and His saying: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43],

• and His saying: ﴿dhi al-qurba (the relative)﴾ [an-Nahl: 90], meaning the one who has kinship from the side of the father or the mother, or both together; because giving to the relative is charity and the maintaining of kinship. Al-itā' (giving) means bestowing. One of its two objects is omitted, because the verbal noun has been added to the first object, and the second has been omitted. The original is "and giving to the one who has kinship";

• as in His saying: ﴿And gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives﴾ — the verse [al-Baqarah: 177].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have made a pledge﴾. In this noble verse, Allah, glorified and exalted, commands His servants to fulfil the covenant of Allah when they make a pledge. The apparent meaning of the verse is that it includes all covenants, both between the servant and his Lord and between him and other people. He repeated this in other places, such as His saying in Al-An'am: ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah. This He has enjoined upon you﴾ [Al-An'am: 152], and His saying in Al-Isra: ﴿And fulfil the covenant, for the covenant will be questioned about﴾ [Al-Isra: 34]. We have already discussed this in (Al-An'am).

(p-439) He made clear in other places that whoever breaks the covenant harms only himself, and that whoever fulfils it, Allah will give him a great reward for that. This is in His saying: ﴿So whoever breaks his oath, breaks it only to his own detriment, and whoever fulfils what he has covenanted with Allah – He will give him a great reward﴾ [Al-Fath: 10]. He also made clear in other places that breaking the covenant deserves curse, as in His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 13].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 96:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What is with you will vanish, and what is with Allah is lasting﴾. In this noble verse, He, may He be glorified and exalted, makes clear that what He has of the bliss of Paradise is lasting and does not perish. He clarified this meaning in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud: 108],

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad: 54],

• and His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward, [in which] they will remain forever﴾ [al-Kahf: 2-3],

along with other verses.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We will surely reward those who were patient with their best deeds that they used to do﴾. In this noble verse, He, may He be glorified and exalted, swears that He will surely reward those who were patient with their reward, i.e., the recompense for their deeds, according to the best of what they used to do.

He made clear in other places that it is a reward without reckoning, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [az-Zumar: 10].

Note of caution.

Some scholars deduced from this noble verse that doing what is permissible (mubah) is good, because His saying in this verse: ﴿according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [an-Nahl: 96] is a comparative form (sigha tafdil) which indicates sharing (in the attribute), and obligatory acts are better than recommended acts, and recommended acts are better than permissible acts. Thus they are recompensed according to the best, which is the obligatory and the recommended, without the permissible (which is also good) being included in the comparison. Upon this, the author of Maraqi as-Su'ud followed, in his saying:

؎Whatever our Lord has not forbidden is good, and what is other than it is ugly and reprehensible.

However, good (hasan) is divided into good and better (ahsan). Among this is His saying, may He be exalted, to Musa: ﴿So take it with strength and command your people to take the best of it...﴾ [al-A'raf: 145]. The recompense mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [an-Nahl: 126] is good, and the patience mentioned in His saying: ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ [an-Nahl: 126] is better. Likewise, Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, and Ibn Dhakwan, by one of the two transmissions from him, read this letter: "wa-lanajziyannahum" with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah). The rest read it with the ya', and this is the second transmission of Ibn Dhakwan.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ In this noble verse, exalted and most high is He, mentions that every doer, whether male or female, who does a righteous deed, Allah – exalted and most high is He – swears that He will surely cause him to live a good life, and that He will surely reward him according to the best of what he used to do.

Know first: the Great Qur'an indicates that righteous deeds are those that fulfil three matters:

The first: that it conforms to what the Prophet ﷺ brought, because Allah says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7].

The second: that it be sincerely for Allah, because Allah – exalted and most high is He – says: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5], and ﴿Say, "It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion. So worship what you will other than Him"﴾ [az-Zumar: 14–15].

The third: that it be founded upon the correct creed, because Allah says: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer﴾ [an-Nahl: 97]. He restricted it by faith, and the implication of its opposite is that if he were not a believer, that righteous deed would not be accepted from him.

Allah – exalted and most high is He – has clarified this implication in many verses, such as His saying concerning the deeds of the disbeliever: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23];

and His saying: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did therein will be lost, and worthless is what they used to do﴾ [Hud: 16];

and His saying: ﴿Their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert﴾ [an-Nur: 39];

and His saying: ﴿Their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows forcefully on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18];

along with other verses.

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of "a good life" in this noble verse.

Some people said: life is not good except in Paradise, so this good life is in Paradise, because worldly life is not free of calamities, troubles, illnesses, pains, sorrows and the like. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And indeed, the Last Abode – that is the [true] life, if they only knew﴾ [al-Ankabut: 64], and "the life" here means true life.

And some scholars said: the good life in this noble verse is in this world, by Allah granting His servant success in what pleases Him, and granting him well-being and lawful provision, as Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world [that which is] good and in the Hereafter [that which is] good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201].

The author of this commentary – may Allah pardon him – says: In this noble verse there is an indication that shows the meaning of "a good life" in the verse is his life in this world being good. That indication is that if we suppose that the meaning of "a good life" is his life in Paradise, in the saying ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [an-Nahl: 97], then His saying ﴿and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [an-Nahl: 97] would become a repetition along with it, because that good life is the reward for their deeds. Unlike if we suppose it is in the life of this world; then the meaning becomes: We will cause him to live a good life in this world, and We will reward him in the Hereafter according to the best of what he used to do, which is clear.

This meaning indicated by the Qur'an is supported by the established Sunnah from him ﷺ.

Ibn Kathir – may Allah have mercy on him – said in his tafsir of this noble verse: "The good life encompasses all aspects of comfort from whatever direction. It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and a group [of scholars] that they interpreted it as lawful good provision, and from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib – may Allah be pleased with him – that he interpreted it as contentment; and likewise Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and Wahb ibn Munabbih said [similarly] – up to his saying – al-Dahhak said: it is lawful provision and worship in this world. al-Dahhak also said: it is acting in obedience and being content with it."

"The correct view is that the good life encompasses all of this, as in the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad: ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid narrated to us, Saʿid ibn Abi Ayyub narrated to us, Shurahbil ibn Sharik narrated to me, from Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Hubuli, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Indeed, he has succeeded who embraced Islam, was given sustenance sufficient for him, and Allah made him content with what He gave him.' Muslim narrated it from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid al-Muqri with it. al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Abu Hani', from Abu ʿAli al-Janbi, from Fadalah ibn ʿUbayd: that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'He has succeeded who was guided to Islam, whose living was sufficient, and who was content with it.' al-Tirmidhi said: this is a sound hadith."

Imam Ahmad said: Yazid narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, from Yahya, from Qatadah, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah does not wrong a believer a good deed: he is given for it in this world and rewarded for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he is fed for his good deeds in this world, until when he reaches the Hereafter there is no good deed for him by which he is given anything good." Muslim alone transmitted it. End of quotation from Ibn Kathir.

These hadiths clearly favour the view that the good life is in this world, because His saying ﷺ "has succeeded" (aflaha) indicates that, since whoever attains success attains a good life. Likewise his saying ﷺ "he is given for it in this world" also indicates this. Ibn Kathir only cited the aforementioned hadiths to draw attention to the fact that they favour the stated view. And Allah knows best.

It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that when a statement revolves between emphasis (tawkid) and establishing a new meaning (ta'sis), it is preferred to interpret it as establishing a new meaning. Marāqī al-Suʿūd alludes to this, gathering it along with similar cases in which the more probable of the two possibilities must be given precedence, in his saying:

"Likewise what opposes a weakness, of rootedness and independence;
And of establishing a general or a continuance, the singular and the absolute are among what is chosen;
Likewise the ordering for obligating action, by what has the preponderance among what is probable."

The meaning of the words of the author of Marāqī is that he gives precedence to the preponderant probable meaning of the wording over the less preponderant probable meaning, such as rootedness (ta'sil), for it is given precedence over the addition of a particle: as in ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [ash-Shura: 11], where it is possible that the kaf is an added particle, and it is possible that it is not added; and by "mithl" is meant the essence, as in the Arabs' saying: "Someone like you does not do this," meaning "it is not befitting for you to do this." So the meaning is: "There is nothing like Allah." A parallel of using "mithl" to mean the essence is: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 10], i.e., to the Qur'an itself, not to something else similar to it; and His saying: ﴿Like one who is in darkness﴾ [al-An'am: 122], i.e., like one who is in darkness. And like independence (istiqlal), which is given precedence over implicit supplementation (idmar): as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who wage war… that they be killed or crucified…﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], where many scholars supply unstated conditions, saying: "that they be killed if they kill, or crucified if they kill and take property, or that their hands and feet be cut off if they take property and do not kill…" etc.

The Malikis therefore prefer that the imam is free to choose among the mentioned penalties absolutely, because the independence of the wording is more preponderant than supplying unstated conditions, since the original state is their absence until established by evidence, as we have indicated previously in (al-Ma'idah). Likewise, ta'sis is given precedence over tawkid, and this is the point of evidence: as in His saying: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [ar-Rahman: 59, 61, 63, 65, 67, 69, 71, 73, 75] in (Surat al-Rahman), and His saying: ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 19, 24, 28, 34, 37, 40, 45, 47, 49] (in al-Mursalat). It is said: the repetition of the phrase in both is emphasis, but that it is ta'sis is more preponderant for the reason we mentioned; so the favours in each place are understood as those preceding. It is said: that phrase is of denial, so no phrase is repeated from them. The same is said of (Surat al-Mursalat), so it is understood as referring to the deniers of what was mentioned; it is said each phrase, etc.

Having known this, know that if we understand "a good life" in the verse as the life of this world, then that is ta'sis. If we understand it as the life of Paradise, then it is repeated together with His following saying: ﴿and We will surely reward them with their reward﴾ [an-Nahl: 97], because the good life of Paradise is their reward, which they are recompensed with.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: The apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [an-Nahl: 97], is that it refers to this world; and this is the view of the majority. And what indicates it is His saying: ﴿and We will surely reward them with their reward﴾ [an-Nahl: 97], meaning in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān﴾. The more apparent of the two opinions regarding this noble verse is that the speech contains an ellipsis of the verb of intention, meaning: "So when you intend to recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah..." to the end of the verse. The intended meaning is not that when he has recited the Qur'an and finished reciting it, he seeks refuge in Allah from the Shayṭān, as might be understood from the apparent wording of the verse, though some scholars have taken this view. The evidence for what we have mentioned is the frequent ellipsis of the verb of intention in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, the context indicating it. Such as His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer...﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Mā'idah: 6], meaning: "when you intend to rise to it," as is evident. And His saying: ﴿When you consult privately, do not consult privately in sin...﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Mujādilah: 9], meaning: "when you intend to consult privately, do not consult privately in sin," because the prohibition concerns only a future matter that is intended to be done, and it is not valid to prohibit an action that has already occurred and passed, as is clear.

The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that seeking refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān is obligatory at the time of recitation, because the form of the imperative (ifʿal) denotes obligation, as established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh).

Many scholars said that the command in the verse denotes recommendation and preference (nadb wa-istiḥbāb). Abū Ja'far Ibn Jarīr (al-Ṭabarī) and others among the imams related a consensus (ijmāʿ) on this. The apparent meaning of the verse also includes the command to seek refuge when reciting in prayer, due to the generality of the verse. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 99:

(p-444) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, exalted and majestic is He, mentions that Satan has no authority over the believers who rely upon Allah, and that his authority is only over his followers who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.

This meaning is explained in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have over them no authority, except those who follow you of the deviators.﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]

• And His saying: ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except of them Your chosen servants.﴾ [al-Hijr: 39-40]

• And His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have over them no authority. And sufficient is your Lord as Disposer of affairs.﴾ [al-Isra': 65]

• And His saying: ﴿And he had over them no authority, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it,﴾ [Saba': 21] to the end of the verse.

• And His saying: ﴿And I had over you no authority, except that I invited you and you responded to me.﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]

The scholars differed regarding the meaning of "authority" (sultan) in this verse.

Most of the people of knowledge said: it means proof (hujjah), i.e., Satan has no proof over them for what he calls them to of worshipping idols.

Some said: he has no authority over them, i.e., domination and power to cause them to fall into a sin from which there is no repentance. We have already mentioned this. What is meant by ﴿those who take him as an ally﴾ [al-Nahl: 100] is those who obey him, thus taking him as an ally through obedience.

The most evident of the sayings concerning His saying ﴿and those who associate others with Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 100] is that the pronoun refers to Satan, not to Allah. The meaning of their associating [others] with him is their obedience to him in disbelief and sins, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 60], and His saying about Ibrahim: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan is ever disobedient to the Most Merciful.﴾ [Maryam: 44], and other verses. As for his authority over those who take him as an ally, it is what they have granted him over themselves of obedience, following, and allegiance, without any justification that would necessitate that.

Note.

It has been said: Allah has established for Satan authority over his allies in verses, such as His saying here: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally. . .﴾ (p-445) [al-Nahl: 100], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have over them no authority, except those who follow you of the deviators.﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. The exception indicates that he has authority over those who follow him of the deviators, while He has negated authority over them in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a party of the believers.﴾ ﴿And he had over them no authority﴾ [Saba': 20-21] to the end of the verse.

And His saying, exalted is He, quoting him and affirming it: ﴿And I had over you no authority, except that I invited you and you responded to me.﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

The answer is that the authority He established for him over them is other than the authority He negated, and that is from two aspects:

The first: the authority established for him is the authority of misguiding them through his adornment [of sin], while the authority negated is the authority of proof. Iblis had no proof through which he could dominate them, but he called them and they responded to him without proof or evidence. The use of "authority" to mean "proof" is frequent in the Qur'an.

The second: Allah did not make for him any authority over them from the outset at all; rather, they are the ones who empowered him over themselves through their obedience to him and their entering into his party. Thus he did not dominate them by force, because Allah says: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak.﴾ [al-Nisa': 76]. He only dominated them by their own will and choice.

The scholar Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned this answer with both its aspects, and we have explained this in our book (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab).

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾ [An-Nahl: 100], and so on.

This noble verse explicitly states that Satan (al-Shaytan) has authority over his allies. Its counterpart is the exception in His saying: ﴿Indeed, over My servants you have no authority, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ [Al-Hijr: 42].

Some verses indicate the negation of his authority over them, such as His saying: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a party of the believers. And he had no authority over them﴾ [Saba': 20-21], and so on.

And His saying, relating His words about him and affirming them: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. And I had no authority over you﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], and so on.

The answer is that the authority which He affirmed for him over them is other than the authority which He negated, and this is from two aspects:

The first: the authority affirmed for him is the authority of misguiding them through his adornment (of falsehood) for them, while the authority negated is the authority of proof (sultan al-hujjah). Iblis had no proof through which he could dominate them, except that he called them and they responded to him without proof or evidence. The use of the word "sultan" for "proof" is frequent in the Qur'an.

The second: Allah did not give him any authority over them at the outset whatsoever, but rather they are the ones who gave him authority over themselves by obeying him and entering into his party. So he did not dominate them by force, because Allah says: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾ (p-321) [An-Nisa': 76], and he only dominated them by their own will and choice. Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned this answer with both of its aspects.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 101 (part 1 of 2):

The Most High said: ﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator." Rather, most of them do not know.﴾ In this noble verse, He—Exalted and Majestic—mentions that when He substitutes a verse in place of another verse, by abrogating a verse or causing it to be forgotten, and brings something better than it or its like, the disbelievers make that a cause for slandering the Messenger (ﷺ), claiming that he is a liar against Allah, a fabricator against Him. They assume that abrogation of a verse by a verse entails al-bada' (a new opinion arising anew), which they hold to be impossible for Allah. Thus they understand from this that the Prophet (ﷺ) is a fabricator against Allah, claiming that had it been from Allah He would have confirmed and established it, and no new opinion would have arisen regarding it so as to abrogate it.

The evidence that His saying ﴿We substitute a verse in place of another verse﴾ [an-Nahl: 101] means "We abrogate a verse and cause it to be forgotten" is His saying: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or its like﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106], and His saying: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget, except what Allah wills﴾ [al-A'la: 6–7], meaning: that you forget it.

The evidence that if He abrogates a verse or causes it to be forgotten, He must bring a replacement better than it or its like is His saying: ﴿We bring one better than it or its like﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106], and His saying here: ﴿We substitute a verse in place of another verse﴾ [an-Nahl: 101].

As for what the polytheists and the Jews claim, that abrogation is impossible for Allah because it entails al-bada', which is a new opinion, it is manifestly baseless and clearly false to every rational person. For abrogation does not entail al-bada' at all. Rather, Allah—Exalted and Majestic—legislates a ruling while knowing that its benefit will expire at a specified time, and that at that time He will abrogate that ruling and replace it with a new ruling in which the benefit lies. When that specified time comes, He—Exalted and Majestic—carries out what was in His prior knowledge concerning the abrogation of that ruling, whose benefit has ceased, in favor of the new ruling in which the benefit lies. Just as the occurrence of illness after health and its reverse, and the occurrence of wealth after poverty and its reverse, and the like, do not entail al-bada', because Allah knows that His divine wisdom requires that change at its specified time, in accordance with what preceded in His eternal knowledge, as is clear.

Allah—Exalted and Majestic—has indicated His knowledge of the cessation of benefit from the abrogated ruling and its being purely in the abrogating ruling by His saying here: ﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ [an-Nahl: 101],
• and His saying: ﴿We bring one better than it or its like. Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106],
• and His saying: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget, except what Allah wills. Indeed He knows what is apparent and what is hidden﴾ [al-A'la: 6–7]. His saying ﴿Indeed He knows what is apparent and what is hidden﴾ [al-A'la: 7], after His saying ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ [al-A'la: 7], indicates that He is most knowing of what He sends down. He knows the benefit of the human being, and the benefit of substituting the new for the first, which was forgotten.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse:

The first issue: There is no disagreement among the Muslims regarding the permissibility of abrogation, rationally and legally, nor regarding its actual occurrence. As for the one who is reported to have disagreed in this, such as Abu Muslim al-Isfahani—he only meant that abrogation is a specification of the time of the ruling by a new address, since the apparent sense of the first address is the continuation of the ruling throughout all time, and the second address indicates the specification of the first ruling to the time before the abrogation. Thus, for him, abrogation is not the lifting of the first ruling. He alluded to this in Maraqi al-Su'ud in his definition of abrogation:

"Lifting of a ruling, or clarification of the time, by an explicit Qur'an or by the Sunnah."

Only the Jews and some of the polytheists disagreed with this, claiming that it entails al-bada', as we have explained. From here the Jews said: the law of Musa is impossible to abrogate.

* *

The second issue: The abrogation of a legal ruling is not valid except by revelation from the Book or the Sunnah, because Allah—Exalted and Majestic—says: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." Say, "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I follow only what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day."﴾ [Yunus: 15]. By this you know that abrogation by reason alone is prohibited. Likewise there is no abrogation by consensus, because consensus is not concluded except after his death (ﷺ), since as long as he is alive the reference is to his saying, doing, and approval (ﷺ), and there is no authority in the consensus of the community alongside him, because following him is an obligation upon everyone. Therefore the definition of consensus must be restricted to being after his death (ﷺ), as the author of Maraqi said in defining consensus:

"It is the agreement of the mujtahids of the community after the death of Ahmad."

After his death, abrogation ceases, because it is legislation, and there is no legislation at all after his death (ﷺ). To the fact that reason and consensus alone cannot validly effect abrogation, Maraqi al-Su'ud also alluded in its statement on abrogation:

"It is not by reason, nor by bare consensus, but it is traced back to its basis."

His saying "but it is traced back to its basis" means that when the scholars' statements say that a text was abrogated by consensus, they mean only that it was abrogated by the text which is the basis of the consensus, not by consensus itself, due to what we mentioned regarding the prohibition of abrogation by it legally. Likewise, it is not permissible to abrogate revelation by analogy (qiyas), according to the careful view. He alluded to this in Maraqi with his saying:

"And among it is abrogating a text by analogy, which is what most people have approved."

That is: and this is the truth.

* *

The third issue: Know that what some of the scholars of legal theory among the Malikis, Shafi'is and others say—that abrogation may occur without a replacement, which some attributed to the majority, and on which Maraqi proceeded with his saying: "The light is abrogated by what is heavy, and it may come devoid of a replacement"—is without doubt false. It is astonishing that such a view was held by great scholars despite their number, since it explicitly contradicts His saying: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or its like﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. There is then no statement at all for anyone after the speech of Allah: ﴿And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?﴾ [an-Nisa': 122], ﴿And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ [an-Nisa': 87], ﴿Are you more knowing or is Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. In this noble verse He—Exalted and Majestic—linked abrogation with bringing a replacement for the abrogated by way of condition and consequence. It is known that truth and falsehood in a conditional proposition attach to the linkage; so it follows that whenever abrogation occurs, bringing something better than the abrogated or its like occurs, as is evident.

As for what some scholars claim—that abrogation occurred in the Qur'an without a replacement, namely in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger, present before your consultation a charity﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 12], which was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Are you apprehensive about presenting charities before your consultation?﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 13 / al-Anfal: 13 as cited] and there is no replacement for this abrogated ruling—

The answer: it has a replacement, namely that the obligation of presenting charity before consultation, when it was abrogated, the recommendation and encouragement of charity remained as a replacement for the abrogated obligation, as is evident.

* *

The fourth issue: Know that it is permissible to abrogate the lighter by the heavier, and the heavier by the lighter. An example of abrogating the lighter by the heavier: the abrogation of the option between fasting and feeding, stated in His saying: ﴿And for those who are able to fast, a ransom: feeding a poor person﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], by something heavier, namely the specific obligation of fasting in His saying: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. And the confinement of adulteresses in houses, stated by His saying: ﴿Confine them to the houses﴾ [an-Nisa': 15], was abrogated by something heavier, namely flogging and stoning: flogging stated in His saying: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress—flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [an-Nur: 2], and stoning by the verse of stoning whose recitation was abrogated while its ruling remained valid, which is His saying: "The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise."

An example of abrogating the heavier by the lighter: the abrogation of the obligation for a Muslim to stand against ten of the disbelievers, stated in His saying: ﴿If there are among you twenty patient ones, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 65], by something lighter, namely the obligation for a Muslim to stand against two of them, stated in His saying: ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden, and He knows that among you is weakness. So if there are among you a hundred patient ones, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 66]. And like the abrogation of His saying: ﴿And if you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], by His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]; this is abrogation of the heavier by the lighter, as is evident. And like the abrogation of the waiting period of a widow by a year, stated in His saying: ﴿And those who are taken in death among you and leave wives—a bequest for their wives: provision for a year without expulsion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240], by something lighter, namely the waiting period of four months and ten days, stated in His saying: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives—they shall wait by themselves four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234].

Admonition.

Know that in His saying—Exalted and Majestic—﴿We bring one better than it or its like﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106] there is a difficulty from two aspects:

The first: it may be said: either the heavier is better than the lighter, because it has greater reward, or the lighter is better than the heavier, because it is easier and closer to the capacity for compliance. If the heavier is better, that requires prohibiting its abrogation by the lighter; and if the lighter is better, that requires prohibiting its abrogation by the heavier, since Allah stated that He brings what is better than the abrogated or equal to it, not what is less. And you have known that the actual practice is the permissibility of abrogating each of them by the other.

The second aspect of the difficulty in His saying ﴿or its like﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]: it may be asked: what is the wisdom in abrogating a like in order to replace it with a like? And what superiority does the like have over the like that it should be abrogated and replaced by it?

The answer to the first difficulty: superiority sometimes lies in the heavier because of greater reward, and this is when the reward is very great and compliance is not extremely difficult, as in the abrogation of the option between feeding and fasting by the obligation of fasting. For fasting carries great reward, as in the sacred hadith: "Except fasting, for it is for Me, and I will reward it." And those who fast are among the best of the patient, since they have been patient for Allah against the desire of their bellies and their private parts; and Allah says: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [az-Zumar: 10]. The hardship of fasting is ordinary, with no severe difficulty that would make one likely unable to comply; and if something that requires it occurs, such as illness or travel, the facilitation through the concession of breaking the fast is stated in His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey—then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. Sometimes superiority lies in the lighter, and this is when the heavier abrogated ruling is extremely difficult, such that compliance is hard; then the lighter is better than it, because the likelihood of non-compliance exposes the responsible person to falling into what does not please Allah. An example is His saying: ﴿And if you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. Had accountability for the passing thoughts of the heart not been abrogated, compliance would have been extremely difficult and burdensome upon souls, hardly safe from falling short in it except for one whom Allah protects. There is no doubt that the abrogation of that by His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286] is better for the responsible person than the continuation of that burdensome ruling. And so on.

The answer to the second objection is that His saying "or one like it" means the similarity between the abrogating and the abrogated ruling in themselves. It does not rule out that the abrogating ruling may entail benefits external to its own essence, by which it is better than the abrogated one. So, considered in its own essence, the abrogating ruling is similar to the abrogated one, while considered in terms of the benefits it entails, which are not found in the abrogated ruling, it is better than the abrogated one.

Its clarification is that most commentators illustrate His saying "or one like it" with the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis by facing the Sacred House of Allah. This abrogating and abrogated ruling are similar when considered in themselves, because each of them is a direction among directions, and in their true nature they are equal. Thus it is not impossible that the abrogating ruling includes wisdoms external to its essence that make it better than the abrogated ruling in that respect. Facing the Sacred House of Allah entails several outcomes, which the Qur'an points to, that do not exist in facing Bayt al-Maqdis. Among them: by it, the argument of the disbelievers of Makkah against the Prophet (ﷺ) falls away, when they said: "You claim that you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, yet you do not face his qiblah!" And by it the argument of the Jews falls away, when they said: "You criticize our religion and face our qiblah, and our qiblah is part of our religion!" And by it also the argument of the Jewish scholars falls away, for they have in the Torah that he (ﷺ) would be commanded to face Bayt al-Maqdis and then be commanded to turn from it to face the Sacred House of Allah. Had he not been commanded to do so, they would have argued against him with what is in their Torah, that he would be turned to the Sacred House of Allah, and the premise is that he was not turned.

Allah, Exalted is He, has pointed to these wisdoms, which are the refutation of these false arguments, in His saying: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150]. Then He explained the wisdom by His saying: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you⁠﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 150]. The dropping of these arguments is among the motives that moved him (ﷺ) to love the turning toward the Sacred House of Allah, which is alluded to in the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque⁠﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 144].

* *

Fifth issue: Know that abrogation (naskh) is of three kinds:

(p-451) The first: the abrogation of both the recitation and the ruling together. Its example is what is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of ʿAishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "Among what was revealed of the Qur'an was ten known sucklings that make marriage prohibited..." — the hadith. So the verse of the ten sucklings is abrogated in both recitation and ruling, by consensus.

The second: the abrogation of the recitation while the ruling remains. Its example is the verse of stoning mentioned above, and the verse of five sucklings according to the opinion of al-Shafiʿi, ʿAishah, and those who agree with them.

The third: the abrogation of the ruling while the recitation remains. This is the most common kind of abrogation in the Qur'an, such as the verse on steadfastness in fighting, the waiting period, the option between fasting and feeding, and the confinement of adulterers. As we mentioned all of this above.

* *

Sixth issue: Know that there is no disagreement among scholars about the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Qur'an and the abrogation of the Sunnah by the mutawatir Sunnah. They differed about the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah, and the reverse, and about the abrogation of the mutawatir by the solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad); their disagreement on these issues is well known. Among those who said that the Book is not abrogated except by the Book, and that the Sunnah is not abrogated except by the Sunnah, is al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that both the Book and the Sunnah are abrogated by each other, because all of it is revelation from Allah, the Exalted. The example of the abrogation of the Sunnah by the Book is the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis by facing the Sacred House of Allah. The facing of Bayt al-Maqdis at first occurred by the Sunnah, not by the Qur'an, and Allah abrogated it by the Qur'an in His saying: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased⁠﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 144]. The example of the abrogation of the Book by the Sunnah is the abrogation of the verse of the ten sucklings in both recitation and ruling by the mutawatir Sunnah. And the abrogation of Surat al-Khal' and Surat al-Hafd in both recitation and ruling by the mutawatir Sunnah. Surat al-Khal' and Surat al-Hafd are the qunut in the dawn prayer according to the Malikis. The author of Ad-Durr al-Manthur and others have clarified the verification that they were two surahs of the Book of Allah, which were then abrogated.

We have already put forward in (Surat al-Anʿam) that what appears to us to be correct is that authentic solitary reports may abrogate the mutawatir, if their being later than it is established, and that there is no contradiction between them, because the mutawatir is true, and the Sunnah that comes after it only explains something new that did not exist before. So there is absolutely no contradiction between them, because their times differ.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure, or [that which is] profane, [over which] the name of other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful⁠﴾ the verse [al-Anʿam: 145].

This indicates, by the indication of correspondence (dalalat al-mutabaqah), a clear indication of the permissibility of the flesh of domestic donkeys, because of the clarity of the restriction by negation and affirmation in the verse concerning that. When the Prophet (ﷺ) then declared, after that, on the day of Khaybar, in an authentic hadith: "Indeed the flesh of domestic donkeys is not permitted," there is absolutely no contradiction between that authentic hadith and that verse revealed years before it, because the hadith indicated a new prohibition, while the verse did not deny the occurrence of anything new in the future, as is clear.

So the verification, if Allah wills, is the permissibility of abrogating the mutawatir by authentic solitary reports whose lateness relative to it is established, even though most of the scholars of usul (usuliyyin) disagreed with this. The author of Maraqi al-Saʿud, in agreement with the majority, followed the opposite view, saying:
"Abrogation of the Book by solitary reports is not, correctly, something that occurs."

From here you know that there is no evidence for the invalidity of the view of the one who said that the bequest to parents and relatives is abrogated by the hadith: "There is no bequest to an heir." And Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

Seventh issue: Know that the verification is that abrogation is permissible before it is possible to act upon the ruling. If it is said: What is the benefit of legislating a ruling first if it will be abrogated before one is able to act upon it?

The answer: the wisdom is to test the responsible persons with the determination to comply. This is clarified by the fact that Allah commanded Ibrahim to slaughter his son, and then abrogated this ruling by ransoming him with a great sacrifice before he was able to carry out the act. He explained that the wisdom in that was the trial, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice⁠﴾ [al-Saffat: 106–107]. Among the examples of abrogation before the possibility of acting is the abrogation of forty-five prayers on the night of the Isra', after fifty prayers had been enjoined, as is well known. He pointed to this issue in Maraqi al-Su'ud by his saying:
"Abrogation before the act has occurred has come, occurring in sound transmission."

* *

Eighth issue: Know that the verification is that not every addition to the text is abrogation, although Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, disagreed on this. Rather, addition to the text is of two kinds. One kind contradicts the text mentioned before it, and this addition is abrogation according to the verification, like adding the prohibition of domestic donkeys and every fanged predator, for example, to the four prohibited things mentioned in the verse: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it⁠﴾ the verse [al-Anʿam: 145]. This is because the domestic donkeys and the like were not left silent about in the verse; rather the requirement of the restriction by negation and affirmation in His saying: ﴿in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion⁠﴾ the verse, is explicit in permitting the domestic donkeys and what is mentioned with them. So that adding their prohibition is abrogation is an obvious matter.

The other kind is where the addition does not contradict the text, but is the addition of something the first text was silent about. This is not abrogation, but the explanation of the ruling of something that was left unmentioned. Such as the exile of the unmarried adulterer, and the ruling by one witness and an oath in property matters. In the first case, the Qur'an enjoined flogging and was silent about anything other than it, so the Prophet (ﷺ) added a ruling about which it was silent, which is exile. Likewise, in the second case, the Qur'an says: ﴿But if they are not two men, then a man and two women⁠﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 282], and it was silent about the ruling of one witness and an oath, so the Prophet (ﷺ) added a ruling about which it was silent. To this point the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud pointed by his saying:
"Not every addition these provide is abrogation, in what was established by the text, except an increase."

We have already put forward in (Surat al-Anʿam), in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden⁠﴾ the verse [al-Anʿam: 145].

He said, ﴿And We know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him."﴾ In this noble verse, He, exalted is He, swears that He knows the disbelievers say that this Qur'an, which the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, is not a revelation from Allah, and that he learned it only from a human being among the people.

He clarified this meaning in another place, such as His saying, ﴿And they say, "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ [al-Furqan: 5], and His saying, ﴿This is nothing but magic transmitted from others﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 24], meaning: Muhammad (ﷺ) narrates it from someone else, and His saying, ﴿And that they may say, "You have studied"﴾ [al-An'am: 105], as was mentioned earlier in (al-An'am).

The scholars differed in identifying this human being whom they claimed was teaching the Prophet (ﷺ). The Qur'an has stated explicitly that he was of a non-Arabic tongue (a'jami al-lisan). It was said: he was the slave of al-Fakih ibn al-Mughirah, whose name was Jabr, and he was a Christian who then embraced Islam. It was said: his name was Ya'ish, a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, and he used to read non-Arabic books. It was said: he was a slave of the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy. It was said: they were two slaves, one named Yasar and the other named Jabr, and they were sword-polishers who made swords, and they used to read a book of theirs. It was said: they used to read the Torah and the Gospel, along with other sayings.

Exalted is He has shown their lying and obstinacy in their saying, ﴿It is only a human being who teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], by His saying, ﴿The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Nahl: 103]. That is: how could his learning come from that human being, when that human being is of a non-Arabic tongue? This Qur'an is clear, eloquent Arabic, with no trace of foreignness in it. So this is unreasonable.

He also showed the extremity of their obstinacy: that even if He had made the Qur'an non-Arabic, they would still have denied it and said, "How can this Qur'an be non-Arabic when the Messenger to whom it was sent is Arab?" This is in His saying, ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained? Is it non-Arabic and Arab?"﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. That is: is it a non-Arabic Qur'an and an Arab Messenger? So how do they deny that the Qur'an is non-Arabic while the Messenger is Arab, yet not deny that the supposed teacher is non-Arabic, though the Qur'an they claim he taught is Arabic?

He also showed their obstinacy by this: that if this clear Arabic Qur'an had been sent down upon a non-Arab, and he recited it to them in Arabic, they would still have denied it, despite that extraordinary matter, due to the severity of their stubbornness and obstinacy. This is in His saying, ﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it to them, they would not have believed in it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 198-199].

His saying in this noble verse, "yulhidun", means they deviate from the truth. The meaning of "the tongue of the human being to whom they deviate" is: they incline their speech away from truth and uprightness towards him; it is a non-Arabic tongue, not clear. While this Qur'an is a clear Arabic tongue, meaning: possessing clarity and eloquence.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this word as "yalhadun", with the ya' and ha' vowelled with fatha, from the triliteral "lahada". The rest read "yulhadun", with the ya' and ha' vowelled with damma, from the triliteral "lahuda". The rest also read "yulhidun", with the ya' vowelled with damma and the ha' with kasra, from the quadriliteral "alhada". These are two dialects, and the meaning is one: that is, (p-455) they incline away from the truth towards falsehood. As for "yulhidun" in (al-A'raf) and in (Fussilat), only Hamzah alone read them with fatha on the ya' and ha', not al-Kisa'i. Al-Kisa'i agreed with him only in this one in (al-Nahl), and applied "tongue" to the Qur'an, because the Arabs use "tongue" and mean by it speech, so they make it feminine and masculine. From this is the saying of A'sha Bahila:

"Verily, a tongue has come to me, which I do not conceal, from a height, there is no wonder in it nor mockery."

And the saying of another:

"A tongue of evil brings it to us, and you betrayed, and I did not think you would betray."

And the saying of another:

"A tongue of the Banu 'Amir came to me, its stories after a strange speech."

From this is His saying, ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later ones﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84], meaning: a good and lasting praise. And from the use of "tongue" in the sense of speech in the masculine is the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

"I regret a tongue that escaped from me, would that it were in a bag of baggage."

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 112 (part 1 of 2):

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah sets forth a parable: a town that was secure and at peace, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. But it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do.﴾ Some scholars said: "This is a parable that Allah set forth for the people of Makkah." This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Qatadah, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam held this view. Malik related it from al-Zuhri, may Allah have mercy on them all. Ibn Kathir and others transmitted it from them.

The attributes mentioned of this town agree with the attributes of the people of Makkah mentioned in the Qur'an. His words about this town, ﴿was secure and at peace﴾ [al-Nahl: 112], are similar to what He said about the people of Makkah:

• As in His words: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ and the verse [al-Qasas: 57],
• And His words: ﴿Do they not see that We made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away all around them?﴾ and the verse [al-'Ankabut: 67],
• And His words: ﴿and gave them security from fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4],
• And His words: ﴿Whoever enters it is secure﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97],
• And His words: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for people and a sanctuary﴾ and the verse [al-Baqarah: 125],
• And His words: ﴿its provision coming to it abundantly from every place﴾ [al-Nahl: 112]. He likewise said something similar about the people of Makkah:
• As in His words: ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾ [al-Qasas: 57],
• And His words: ﴿For the covenant of the Quraysh, their covenant of the journey of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and gave them security from fear﴾ [Quraysh: 1–4]. The winter journey was to Yemen and the summer journey was to Syria, and wealth and provision came to them from both journeys. Therefore He followed the two journeys with His favour upon them: that He fed them against hunger.
• And His words in the supplication of Ibrahim: ﴿And when Ibrahim said: "My Lord, make this a secure town and provide its people with fruits"﴾ and the verse [al-Baqarah: 126],
• And His words: ﴿So make hearts from among the people incline towards them and provide them with fruits﴾ and the verse [Ibrahim: 37].

His words, ﴿But it denied the favours of Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 112], He mentioned something similar about the people of Makkah in many verses, such as His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favour of Allah for ingratitude and caused their people to alight in the abode of destruction?﴾ [Ibrahim: 28].

We have already presented a part of this in discussing His words: ﴿They recognise the favour of Allah, then deny it﴾ and the verse [al-Nahl: 83].

His words, ﴿so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 112], something similar to it definitely happened to the people of Makkah when they persisted in disbelief and obstinacy, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked against them and said: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them years like the years of Yusuf." So a drought struck them that destroyed everything, until they ate carrion and al-'Ilhiz (which is the wool of a camel mixed with its blood when they slaughtered it). And severe fear struck them after security. That fear was from the armies of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his military campaigns, his expeditions and his detachments. This hunger and fear, the Qur'an pointed to them according to some interpretations. Ibn Mas'ud interpreted the verse of (al-Dukhan) in a way that indicates this.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: Chapter: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10]. "Watch" [al-Dukhan: 10]: wait. 'Abdan narrated to us, from Abu Hamzah, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, from Masruq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: Five have passed: the smoke, the Romans, the moon, the striking, and the grip. ﴿It covers the people; this is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11]. Yahya narrated to us, Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, from Masruq, who said: "'Abd Allah said: 'This only happened because the Quraysh, when they disobeyed the Prophet ﷺ, he invoked against them with years like the years of Yusuf. So a famine and hardship struck them, until they ate bones. A man would look at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke, from hardship.' So Allah the Exalted sent down: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ ﴿It covers the people; this is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10, 11]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was approached and it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah for rain for Mudar, for they have perished!' He said: 'For Mudar! You are indeed bold!' So he asked for rain and they were given rain. Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. When comfort came to them, they returned to their former state when comfort had come to them. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿On the day We will strike with the greatest striking; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16], meaning the Day of Badr."

Chapter of His words: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12]. Yahya narrated to us, Waki' narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, who said: I entered upon 'Abd Allah and he said: "Indeed, from knowledge is that you say of what you do not know: 'Allah knows best.' Indeed Allah said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Say: I do not ask of you any wage for it, nor am I of the pretenders﴾ [Sad: 86]." When the Quraysh overcame the Prophet ﷺ and disobeyed him, he said: "O Allah, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Yusuf." So a year struck them in which they ate bones and carrion from hardship, until one of them would look at what was between him and the sky and see something like smoke from hunger. They said: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12]. It was said to him: "If We remove it from them, they will return." So he invoked his Lord and He removed it from them, and they returned. So Allah took retribution upon them on the Day of Badr. That is His saying: ﴿On the day the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10], up to His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]." End of quotation in its wording from Sahih al-Bukhari.

In the tafsir of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, of this noble verse there is clear indication that the hunger that this town mentioned in (Surah al-Nahl) was made to taste was tasted by the people of Makkah, until they ate bones, and a man among them would imagine something like smoke from the intensity of hunger. This interpretation from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, has the ruling of being traced to the Prophet ﷺ (marfu'), because it is established in the science of hadith that a companion's interpretation which is connected to the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) has the ruling of being traced to the Prophet ﷺ. As the author of Talhat al-Anwar indicated with his words:

"The interpretation of a companion connected to the occasion, its elevation is verified."

As is well known among the scholars.

We have already presented that in (Surah al-Baqarah) in the discussion of His words: ﴿So approach them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222].

It is established in Sahih Muslim that smoke is one of the signs of the Hour. There is no obstacle to carrying the noble verse on both smokes: the smoke that has passed and the smoke yet to come, combining the evidences. We have already presented that when there are multiple interpretations of a verse, if it is possible to carry the verse on all of them, that is preferable. We have already presented that this is what Abu al-'Abbas ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, verified in his treatise on the sciences of the Qur'an, with his evidences.

As for the fear mentioned in the verse of "al-Nahl," He, Mighty and Exalted, also mentioned its like about the people of Makkah, according to some interpretations of the noble verse which is: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve because of what they have done, or it will settle near their home﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. It has been reported from a group of the early scholars (salaf) that the disaster that strikes them is a military expedition from the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The author of al-Durr al-Manthur said: Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding His words: ﴿Disaster will strike them because of what they have done﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], he said: "The expeditions." Al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported through the chain of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding His words: "﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], he said: 'A detachment'. ﴿Or it will settle near their home﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], he said: 'You, O Muhammad, until the promise of Allah comes.' He said: 'The conquest of Makkah.'" Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding His words: "﴿Disaster will strike them because of what they have done﴾, he said: 'A detachment from the detachments of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. ﴿Or it will settle﴾: O Muhammad, near their home.'" Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The disaster is the expeditions. ﴿Or it will settle near their home﴾, he said: 'Al-Hudaybiyyah.' ﴿Until the promise of Allah comes﴾, he said: 'The conquest of Makkah.'" Ibn Jarir reported from 'Ikrimah, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding His words: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve﴾, the verse: it was revealed in Madinah concerning the expeditions of the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿Or it will settle, O Muhammad, near their homes﴾. End of the relevant point from it.

This interpretation mentioned in the verse of (al-Ra'd), and the interpretation mentioned before it in the verse of (al-Dukhan), indicate that the people of Makkah were exchanged, after abundance of provision, for hunger, and after security and tranquillity, for fear, as He said about the town mentioned: ﴿It was secure and at peace, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. But it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 112]. And His words about the town mentioned: ﴿And there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him﴾ ... the verse [al-Nahl: 113]. It is not hidden that He said the like of this about the Quraysh in many verses, such as His words: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ and the verse [al-Tawbah: 128], and His words: ﴿Certainly did Allah confer favour upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from themselves﴾ and the verse [Al 'Imran: 164].

The verses explicitly stating their disbelief and obstinacy are very numerous, such as His words: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a astonishing thing!﴾ ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, [saying]: "Walk on and remain steadfast to your gods..."﴾ the verse [Sad: 5], [p. 459] and His words: ﴿And when they see you, they take you not except in ridicule: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger? He would have almost led us astray from our gods had we not remained steadfast to them."﴾ and the verse [al-Furqan: 41–42]. Verses like these are very numerous.

Thus, the totality of what we have mentioned supports the view of the one who said that what is meant by this town set forth as a parable in this verse of (al-Nahl) is Makkah. It was narrated from Hafsah and others that it is Madinah, and she said that when news of the killing of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, reached her. Some scholars said: it is an unspecified town, which Allah set forth as a parable to frighten against opposing the favour of security, tranquillity, and provision with disbelief and transgression. Those who held this view said that the indefiniteness of "a town" in the noble verse indicates it, in His words: ﴿And Allah sets forth a parable: a town﴾ and the verse [al-Nahl: 112].

The author of this note, may Allah pardon him, said: In any case, every intelligent person must take a lesson from this parable, and not oppose the favours of Allah with disbelief and transgression, lest there befall him what befell this mentioned town. But parables are not understood from Allah except by those whom Allah has given knowledge, according to His words: ﴿And these are the parables We set forth for the people, but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].
