Regarding His words in this noble verse, "a town," there are two aspects of i'rab (grammatical analysis).

One: that it is a substitute (badal) for His words "a parable." The second: that "set forth" (daraba) is taken to imply "made" (ja'ala), and "a town" is the first object, and "a parable" is the second object. "A town" was placed later so that there would be no separation between it and its mentioned attributes in His words: "was secure..." etc.

And His words in this noble verse, "at peace" (mutma'innah), meaning: no fear disturbs it, because tranquillity goes with security, and agitation and anxiety go with fear.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 112 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, "raghadan" (ample, pleasant), means: abundant and delicious. As for "al-an'um" (the bounties), it is said to be the plural of "ni'mah" (blessing), like "shiddah" and "ashuddah." Or it is the plural without the feminine ta' being counted, like "dir'" (coat of mail) and "adru'" (plural). Or it is the plural of "nu'm," like "bu's" (hardship) and "ab'us" (plural), as has preceded in (Surat al-An'am) in the discussion of His saying: ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾ (Qur'an 6:152).

In this noble verse there is a well-known question, which is to say: how did He attribute tasting (idhaqah) to clothing (libas) in His saying: ﴿So Allah made them taste the clothing of hunger and fear﴾ (Qur'an 16:112)? It is related that Ibn al-Rawandi, the heretic (zindiq), said to Ibn al-A'rabi, the imam of language and literature: "Can clothing be tasted?!" He intended to criticize (al-ta'n) the words of the Exalted: ﴿So Allah made them taste the clothing of hunger﴾, the verse. Ibn al-A'rabi said to him: "No harm, O you nasnas (a deformed being)! Suppose Muhammad (ﷺ) was not a prophet. Was he not an Arab?"

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The answer to this question is clear, namely that He applied the name of clothing to what befell them of hunger and fear, because the traces of hunger and fear appear on their bodies and envelop them like clothing. Because they experience that clothing, which is expressed by the traces of hunger and fear, He attributed tasting to it. Therefore there is no need for the figures of speech that the rhetoricians (al-bayaniyyun) mention regarding this noble verse. We have clarified in our treatise that we named (Man' Jawaz al-Majaz fi al-Manzil li-l-Ta'abbud wa-l-I'jaz) (The Prohibition of Permitting Metaphor in the Revealed Text for Worship and Inimitability) that it is not permissible for anyone to say that there is metaphor (majaz) in the Qur'an. We clarified this with its evidences, and we explained that what the rhetoricians call metaphor is a style (uslub) of the features of the Arabic language.

The rhetoricians have differed regarding this verse. Some of them say: in it there is a pure metaphor (isti'arah mujarradah), meaning that what is used in it is what suits the borrowed-for (al-musta'ar lahu). Their claim is that He borrowed the term clothing for certain events that overtook them, such as hunger and fear, by the common feature of their enveloping them, just as clothing envelops the wearer, by way of the explicit, original, and actual metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tasrihiyyah al-asliyyah al-tahqiqiyyah). Then He mentioned the attribute which is tasting, suited to the borrowed-for, which is hunger and fear, because the application of the word "taste" to the experiencing of hunger and fear has become, in their usage, like the literal meaning due to frequency of use.

They say: "dhaqa al-bu's wa-l-darr" (he tasted misery and harm), and another made him taste them; so the metaphor is pure, in that what suits the borrowed-for, which is the likened (al-mushabbah) in the original comparison which is the basis of the metaphor, is mentioned. If it were intended to make this metaphor a "tarshih" (nurturing) in their claim, it would be said: "fa-kasahā" (then He clothed them), because bringing what suits the borrowed-from, which is the likened-to (al-mushabbah bihi) in the comparison which is the basis of the metaphor, is called "tarshih," and "kiswah" (garment-clothing) suits clothing, so mentioning it is a tarshih of the metaphor. They say: although the nurtured metaphor is more eloquent than the pure one, the pure metaphor in the verse is more eloquent, in that the borrowed-for, which is fear and hunger, has been observed, and by mentioning tasting which suits that, the speech becomes clearer.

Some of them said: it is a metaphor built upon a metaphor. For first, he borrowed the name of clothing for what appears on their bodies of yellowing, withering, and emaciation, by the common feature of encompassing a thing and enveloping it. So the name clothing became borrowed for the traces of hunger and fear on their bodies. Then he borrowed the name of tasting for what they find of the pain of that hunger and fear, expressed by clothing, by the common feature of perception and testing in each of tasting with the mouth and the existence of pain from hunger and fear. Accordingly, in "clothing" there is an original metaphor as we have mentioned, and in the borrowed "tasting" there is, for the sensing of the pain of hunger and fear, a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah).

We have touched here upon a small portion of the rhetoricians' discourse so that the reader may understand their intent, although the truth beyond any doubt is that all of that has no benefit in it and no real worth, and that the Arabs use "idhaqah" for tasting and for other than it, such as the experiencing of pain and pleasure, and they use "libas" for the known (garment), and for other than it of what carries the meaning of clothing in enveloping; such as His saying: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ (Qur'an 2:187), and the saying of al-A'sha:

"When the bedfellow bends her side, she bends upon him and becomes a garment."

All of these are Arabic styles. There is no difficulty in that when the term clothing is applied to a painful effect that envelops the person as clothing envelops, there is no obstacle to attributing tasting to that enveloping pain expressed by the name clothing. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 116:

Allah's words: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to fabricate lies against Allah.﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Exalted, forbids the disbelievers from declaring unlawful what Allah has made lawful of His provision, such as what 'Amr ibn Luhayy (may Allah curse him) prescribed for them of forbidding what Allah had made lawful.

Allah, Mighty and Exalted, has clarified this meaning in many verses, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Say: "Bring forward your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this." If they testify, do not testify with them.﴾ [al-An'am: 150],

• His saying: ﴿Say: "Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you have made of it unlawful and lawful?" Say: "Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?"﴾ [Yunus: 59],

• His saying: ﴿Those have lost who killed their children in foolishness without knowledge and prohibited what Allah had provided for them, fabricating against Allah. They have certainly gone astray and were not guided.﴾ [al-An'am: 140],

• His saying: ﴿And they say, "What is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our females"﴾ [al-An'am: 139], to the end of the verse,

• His saying: ﴿And they say, "These are cattle and crops that are forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we will," by their claim﴾ [al-An'am: 138], to the end of the verse,

and His saying "ḥijr" (forbidden), meaning unlawful, along with other verses, as has preceded.

Regarding His saying "al-kadhib" (the lie) [al-Nahl: 116], there are several grammatical analyses (i'rab):

First: it is in the accusative governed by "taqulu" (say). That is: do not say the lie concerning what your tongues describe of Allah's provision as lawful or unlawful, as mentioned in the verses cited above, without that description being based on any evidence. The "lam" here is like it in your saying: "Do not say of what Allah has made lawful: it is unlawful," and like His saying: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 154] to the end of the verse. The clause ﴿This is lawful and this (p. 462) is unlawful﴾ is in apposition (badal) to "al-kadhib" (the lie). It has also been said that the aforementioned clause occupies the position of an accusative after "taṣifu" (describe), by including within it the meaning of "taqulu" (say). That is: and do not say the lie concerning what your tongues describe, so that you say "This is lawful and this is unlawful." It has also been said that "al-kadhib" is the direct object of "taṣifu," with "mā" being a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), and the clause ﴿This is lawful and this is unlawful﴾ is connected to "lā taqulū." That is: do not say "This is lawful and this is unlawful" on account of your tongues describing the lie; that is, do not prohibit or permit on account of a statement which your tongues utter and which circulates in your mouths, not on account of a proof or clear evidence. This was said by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). It has also been said that "al-kadhib" is a substitute (badal) for the omitted object pronoun of "mā," meaning: for what your tongues describe as the lie.

Note.

The righteous predecessors (may Allah be pleased with them) would abstain from saying "This is lawful and this is unlawful," out of fear of these verses.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this noble verse: al-Darimi, Abu Muhammad, said in his Musnad: Harun narrated to us, from Hafs, from al-A'mash, who said: "I never heard Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) say 'lawful' or 'unlawful.' Rather he would say: 'They used to dislike it, and they used to prefer it.'"

Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: "It was not the custom of the people of legal opinion to say 'This is lawful and this is unlawful.' Rather they would say: 'Beware of such-and-such, and I would not do this.'" End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The "lam" in His saying ﴿so that you fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ [al-Nahl: 116] is of the kind of causation that does not include the meaning of obligation. End of quotation. Many scholars say that it is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah). The rhetoricians (al-bayaniyyun) hold that a particle of causation like "lam," when it is not intended to express a final cause ('illah ghā'iyyah), involves a contiguous metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) in the meaning of the particle, as in His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8] to the end of the verse, and His saying here: ﴿so that you fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ [al-Nahl: 116].

The author of this commentary, (may Allah pardon him), says: Rather, all of that is among the styles of the Arabic language. Among its styles is the use of a particle of causation to indicate a final cause, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance that people may maintain justice﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Hadid: 25]. Among its styles is also the use of "lam" to indicate that one matter follows from another, like the way an effect follows from its final cause. This latter is like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up (p. 463) that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], because the final cause that motivated them to pick him up was not that he would become an enemy to them, but rather that he would be a comfort to their eyes, as the wife of Pharaoh said: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas: 9]. But since his becoming an enemy and a grief to them follows from their picking him up, as an effect follows from its final cause, it was expressed with "lam," which indicates the effect's following from the cause. This is an Arabic style, so there is no need for the rhetoricians to lengthen their discussion on this kind of topic.

* *

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah the lie will not succeed﴾ ﴿A brief enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Exalted, mentions that those who fabricate against Him the lie, that is, who invent it against Him, such as their claim that He has forbidden this when He has not forbidden it, and their claim that He has partners and children, will not succeed. This is because in this world they will attain only a brief enjoyment of no significance, and in the Hereafter they will be punished with a great, severe and painful punishment.

He clarified this meaning in other places, such as:

• His saying in Surah Yunus: ﴿Say: "Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah the lie will not succeed." ﴿A brief enjoyment in this world; then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ [Yunus: 69–70],

• His saying: ﴿We will give them enjoyment for a little, then We will compel them to a severe punishment﴾ [Luqman: 24],

• His saying: ﴿He said, "As for one who disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little; then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126],

along with other verses.

His saying ﴿A brief enjoyment﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: their enjoyment in this world is a brief enjoyment. Al-Zamakhshari said: their benefit in this world is a brief enjoyment. His saying "will not succeed" means they will not attain success (al-falah). This term is used in two senses: the first is attaining the greatest sought-after goal, and the second is everlasting survival, as has preceded with its evidence.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 118:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you before﴾ – the verse. This is what was forbidden to them, the matter related to you before, the one made lawful for them here, is what is mentioned in (Surat al-An'am), in His saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws. And of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs or their entrails carry, or what is mingled with bone. That We repaid them for their rebellion; and indeed, We are truthful﴾ [al-An'am: 164].

The totality of what was forbidden to them in this noble verse is apparent: it is every animal with claws, such as the ostrich and the camel, and pure fat from cattle and sheep – which is the tharub (the fat covering the intestines) – and the fat of the kidneys. As for the fat that is on the back, that which is in the entrails (al-hawaya), which are the intestines, and that which is mingled with bone, such as the fat of the tail and other fats mingled with bones, it is lawful for them, as is clear from the noble verse.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 120:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a leader (ummah), devoutly obedient to Allah, upright (hanif), and he was not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ ﴿grateful for His favors. He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾. In these two noble verses, Allah, exalted is He, praises His prophet Abraham, peace and blessings be upon him and upon our Prophet, by saying that he was an ummah, that is, an imam (leader) to be followed, who teaches people good; as He said: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. And that he was qanit (devoutly obedient) to Allah, that is, obedient to Him; that he was not of those who associate others with Allah; that he was grateful for the favors of Allah; that Allah chose him (ijtaba), that is, selected him and chose him for Himself; and that He guided him to a straight path.

He repeated this praise of him in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his commitments]﴾ [al-Najm: 37],

• His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with commands, and he fulfilled them, He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124],

• His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgment before, and We were of him well-knowing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 51],

• His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain (in faith)﴾ [al-An'am: 75],

• His saying about him: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining (hanif), and I am not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 79],

• His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was inclining (hanif), a Muslim, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67],

• His saying: ﴿And indeed, from among his followers was Abraham, when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 83-84],

and other verses, many in number, that praise him.

We have already mentioned the meanings of "ummah" (ummah) in the Qur'an.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave him good in this world﴾ and the rest of the verse [al-Nahl: 221]. Some scholars said: The good that Allah gave him in this world is the righteous offspring and the good commendation. This is supported by the fact that Allah explained that He gave him righteous offspring because of his sincerity to Allah and his withdrawal from the people of polytheism. He also indicated it, since He made for him an enduring good commendation in this world. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when he had removed himself from them and what they worshipped other than Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each We made a prophet﴾ ﴿And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy and made for them a tongue of truth, [and] high﴾ [Maryam: 49-50]. He said: ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Scripture﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 27]. And He said: ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84].

(p-465) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], "Follow the religion of Ibrahim, inclining toward truth; and he was not of those who associate others with Allah."﴾ In this noble verse, Allah - exalted is He - mentions that He revealed to Our Prophet ﷺ the command to follow the religion (millah) of Ibrahim, inclining toward truth, and that he was not of those who associate others with Allah.

He also clarified this in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path - a correct religion, the religion of Ibrahim, inclining toward truth; and he was not of those who associate others with Allah."﴾ [al-An'am: 161],

• And His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord and do good that you may succeed.﴾ up to His saying: ﴿the religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ - the verse [al-Hajj: 77-78],

• And His saying: ﴿There has already been for you an excellent pattern in Ibrahim﴾ - the verse [al-Mumtahanah: 4],

in addition to other verses. The millah (religion, sacred law) is the shari'ah (sacred law). The hanif (one who inclines toward truth) is one who turns away from every false religion toward the religion of truth. Its root is from al-hanaf, which is the bowing of the two legs; it is said: "in his leg is hanaf," meaning bowing. From this is the saying of the mother of al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, as she lulled him while he was a child: "By Allah, were it not for the hanaf in his leg, there would not have been among your youths one like him."

His saying "hanifan" (inclining toward truth) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the mudaf ilayhi (the second term of the construct), in accordance with the statement of Ibn Malik in the Khulasah: "Whatever is part of what it is attributed to, or like its part, do not let it be unfavored."

Because the mudaf (the first term of the construct) here, namely millah, is like a part of the mudaf ilayhi, namely Ibrahim; for if it were omitted, the meaning would remain complete, since our saying "follow Ibrahim" is a complete sentence in meaning, as is evident. This is what he means by its being "like its part."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 125:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾, in this noble verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet ﷺ that he should dispute with his opponents in the manner that is the best of the methods of disputation: by making the truth clear with gentleness and leniency. It is related from Mujahid regarding ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾ [an-Nahl: 125] that he said: "Turn away from their harm." This meaning has been indicated in His saying: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the way that is best, except for those of them who have committed injustice﴾ [al-Ankabut: 46], i.e., except for those who have taken up arms against the believers, so argue with them by the sword until they believe, or give the jizyah (the poll tax) willingly while they are humbled.

The like of what has been mentioned here regarding disputation in the way that is best is His saying to Musa and Harun concerning Pharaoh: ﴿So speak to him gently, that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. Among that gentle speech is Musa's saying to him: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself, and I would guide you to your Lord so you would fear Him?﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 18-19].

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾. In this noble verse He, Mighty and Majestic, mentions that He is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, i.e., who has deviated from the path of correctness and truth toward the path of disbelief and misguidance.

This meaning is clarified in other places:

• As in His saying at the beginning of (al-Qalam): ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ [al-Qalam: 7-8],

• and His saying in (al-An'am): ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ [al-An'am: 117],

• and His saying in (an-Najm): ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ [an-Najm: 30],

and verses of this kind are very numerous.

The apparent meaning is that the form of comparison, which is "a'lam" (most knowing), in these verses is intended to denote the absolute attribute and not comparison, because no one shares with Allah in knowledge of what His creatures will come to of wretchedness and happiness. So it is like the saying of ash-Shanfara:

And if hands are stretched out to the provision, I am not the hastiest of them, though the greediest of the people is the hastiest.

i.e., I was not hasty. And the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mighty and lofty.

i.e., mighty and lofty.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished. But if you are patient, it is better for the patient.﴾ This noble verse of (Surat al-Nahl) was revealed at Medina, concerning the mutilation of the polytheists upon Hamza and those who were killed with him on the Day of Uhud. The Muslims said: "If Allah grants us victory over them, we will surely mutilate them." So this noble verse was revealed, and they were patient, in response to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but it is better for the patient﴾ [al-Nahl: 126]. Although Surat al-Nahl is Meccan, these three verses at its end are an exception. The verse contains the permissibility of retaliation and the guidance toward the superiority of pardon. Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned this meaning in the Qur'an;

• such as His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Shura: 40],

• and His saying: ﴿And the wounds are subject to retaliation. But whoever gives [it] as charity, it is an expiation for him﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Ma'ida: 45],

• and His saying: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those — there is no path [of blame] against them﴾ — to His saying — ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [al-Shura: 41–43],

• and His saying: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil in speech except by one who has been wronged﴾ — to His saying — ﴿or you pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ [al-Nisa: 149],

as we have previously mentioned.

* *

(p-467) Issues derived from this noble verse.

The first issue: From this verse is derived the ruling on the matter of self-redress (al-zafar), namely that if a person wrongs you by taking something of your property without a lawful basis, and you cannot prove it, and you are able to inflict upon him the like of what he inflicted upon you, in a manner where you are safe from disgrace and punishment; is it permissible for you to take the amount of your right or not?

The more correct of the two opinions, and the one most in accord with the apparent meanings of the texts and with analogy, is that you may take the amount of your right without excess; based on His saying, exalted is He, in this verse: ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Nahl: 126], and His saying: ﴿So whoever has assaulted you, then assault him in the same manner as he has assaulted you﴾ [al-Baqara: 194].

Among those who said this opinion are Ibn Sirin, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Sufyan, Mujahid, and others.

Yet a group of scholars, including Malik, said: It is not permissible; and Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki followed this in his Mukhtasar with his statement on deposits: "He may not take from them for one who wronged him with their like."

Those who held this view argued with the hadith: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you," end of quote. This hadith, even if authentic, cannot sustain the argument; for whoever takes the amount of his right and does not exceed it has not betrayed the one who betrayed him, but has merely done justice to himself against one who wronged him.

The second issue: Some scholars derived from this noble verse the requirement of equivalence in retaliation (qisas): whoever kills with an iron implement is killed with it, and whoever kills with a stone is killed with it. This is supported by his ﷺ crushing the head of a Jew between two stones as retaliation for a slave girl whom he had done the same to.

This is the view of the majority of scholars, contrary to Abu Hanifa and those who agreed with him, who claimed that killing by other than a sharp instrument is quasi-intentional (shibh 'amd), not outright intentional, so that retaliation is not obligatory for it. Further clarification of this will come, Allah willing, in (Surat al-Isra').

The third issue: In this noble verse, exalted is He, applied the term "punishment" (uqubah) to the first offense, in His saying: ﴿with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], while the first offense is not a punishment; for the Qur'an is in clear Arabic tongue. Among the methods of the Arabic language is the harmonization (al-mushakala) of words: a term is used with a meaning other than its proper meaning because of its pairing with another term connected to it in the speech; like the poet's saying:

"They said: Propose something and we will cook it for you. I said: Cook for me a robe and a shirt."

That is: sew for me. Some scholars said: Among this is Jarir's saying:

"These widows have had their need fulfilled, so who will fulfill the need of this widower male?"

based on the view that "widows" (al-aramil) is used in the language only for women.

Similar to the noble verse in applying one of the two punishments to the initiation of the act, by harmonization with the other term, is His saying: ﴿That [is so]; and whoever punishes with the like of that with which he was punished and then is wronged [again] — Allah will surely support him﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Hajj: 60], and similar to it as well.

His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], although retaliation is not an evil; and His saying: ﴿So whoever has assaulted you, then assault him in the same manner as he has assaulted you﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Baqara: 194]; because retaliation against the aggressor is also not aggression, as is evident, but was expressed with other than its own wording for the harmonization between the two expressions.

The words of His, exalted is He: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but by Allah﴾ and so on [An-Nahl: 127]. In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that he (ﷺ) (ﷺ) is commanded to be patient, and that he cannot carry out this command to be patient except by Allah's help and enabling success for him, because of His words: ﴿And your patience is not but by Allah﴾ and so on [An-Nahl: 127]. He alluded to this meaning in other places, such as His words: ﴿And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35]. For His words: ﴿And none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ and so on, mean that the quality of patience is not attained except by one who has with Allah the greatest fortune and the most abundant share, by Allah's grace upon him and His facilitating that for him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 128:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾. In this noble verse, He - Majestic and Exalted - mentions that He is with His God-fearing and good-doing servants. The clarification of the meaning of taqwa (God-consciousness) and ihsan (excellence in doing good) has already preceded.

This companionship with His believing servants is by way of assistance, victory and granting success. He repeated this meaning in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46],

• And His saying: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "Indeed, I am with you"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12],

• And His saying: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us﴾ [at-Tawbah: 40],

• And His saying: ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 62],

along with other verses.

As for the general companionship with all creation, it is by complete encompassing, knowledge, the penetrating of power, and the whole of creation being in His grip, Majestic and Exalted. The created beings in His hand are smaller than a mustard seed. This is also mentioned in many verses, such as:

• His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them, nor of five but that He is the sixth of them, nor less than that nor more but that He is with them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7] - the verse continues,

• And His saying: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4] - the verse continues,

• And His saying: ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were not absent﴾ [al-A'raf: 7],

• And His saying: ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor recite of it any Qur'an, nor do any deed, but We are witness over you when you are involved in it﴾ [Yunus: 61] - the verse continues,

along with other verses.

He - Majestic and Exalted - is established upon His Throne as He said, in the manner fitting to His perfection and majesty. He encompasses His creation, all of them in the grip of His hand; not an atom's weight in the earth or in the heavens escapes Him, nor anything smaller than that or greater, except that it is in a clear Book.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾.

This noble verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that Allah's companionship is specific to the God-fearing good-doers.

Other verses have come which indicate its generality, namely His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them, nor of five but that He is the sixth of them, nor less than that nor more but that He is with them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7].

And His saying: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4].

And His saying: ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were not absent﴾ [al-A'raf: 7].

And His saying: ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter﴾ [Yunus: 61].

The answer is that Allah has a specific companionship and a general companionship. The specific companionship is by victory, granting success and assistance, and this is for the specific God-fearing good-doers, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him﴾ [an-Nahl: 128].

And His saying: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "Indeed, I am with you"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12].

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46].

And His saying: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us﴾ [at-Tawbah: 40].

And there is a general companionship by encompassing and knowledge, because He, the Exalted, is greater and more magnificent than everything, encompassing everything. All creatures in His hand are smaller than a mustard seed in the hand of one of us, and His is the highest likeness. Further clarification of this will come in surah "al-Hadid", God willing, and it is general to all creation, as the preceding verses indicate.
